profiles.label: BMW M Roadster & M Coupe (Z3 M, E36/7 & E36/8, 1998-2002)
profiles.framing: A characterful fair-weather weekend and daily driver, NOT a collector or investment car. The buyer values reliability, condition, driving engagement, value, and proximity to Carmel / Monterey / Bay Area. All Z3 M cars are factory manual. Identify the engine: 1998-2000 = S52 (more robust); 2001-2002 = S54 (rod-bearing design flaw, VANOS failures common and costly).
profiles.weak_points: REAR SUBFRAME / trunk-floor differential-mount cracking or tearing (worst on the M; inspect from below AND the trunk spot welds; reinforcement plates are the fix). S54: rod bearings (preventive replacement with upgraded bearings + oil analysis), double-VANOS failures. S52: cooling system, VANOS rattle. Finned differential mounts. Valve-cover and oil filter housing leaks. Rear trailing-arm bushings. Window regulators. Convertible-top mechanism (roadster). Cluster pixels. Cracked dashboard. Rust at rockers/floors.
profiles.immediate_repairs: cooling-system refresh, tires, fluids, oil analysis (S54)
profiles.repairs_12mo: rod bearings (S54, if not documented), VANOS service, rear subframe reinforcement, clutch if worn
profiles.market_notes: M coupes are the most valuable Z3 variant by a wide margin, with S54 coupes at the top. Documented rod-bearing and subframe work materially raises value. Mileage matters less than documentation on these cars.
profiles.catchup_notes: Cooling regardless of mileage; S54 rod bearings; VANOS; motor/trans mounts; rear shock mounts; tires by date; soft top; A/C. Salvage cars need pre/post-loss photos, invoices, the branding reason, measurements, airbag confirmation, CA smog feasibility, and a specialist PPI covering collision repair and the rear structure.

profiles.label: BMW 02 Series (E10: 1600-2 / 2002 / 2002tii)
profiles.framing: This is a 2,200-lb, 100-hp analog sports sedan bought to be driven on Highway 1, Laureles Grade and Carmel Valley Road — not stored. For this buyer the car's value lives in its structure and its paperwork: a sorted, rust-free, honestly documented 2002 is a delightful weekly driver, while a pretty repaint over filled shock towers and spring perches is a five-figure hole. Because nearly every surviving 02 has been modified (Weber 32/36 or 38/38, headers, Ireland/Bilstein suspension, 15-inch wheels), the realistic test is not 'original' but 'reversible, well-chosen, and professionally installed, with the original parts and receipts on hand.' Five-digit odometers and 'Mileage Exceeds Mechanical Limits' titles mean condition and service history — not indicated miles — set the price.
profiles.weak_points: ['Structural rust is the defining failure mode and it is age- not mileage-driven. The front strut/shock towers crack and rot where the tower meets the inner fender and at the spring perches; a car with bubbling or filler here needs $3,000–$10,000+ of metal work. Ask for bare-metal or undercarriage photos of both towers, and press on the perch with a screwdriver during a PPI.', 'Rear subframe mounting points, trailing-arm mounts and the rear shock towers under the parcel shelf rot from trapped water. Failure here is a safety item and is commonly hidden by fresh undercoating. Look for factory seam sealer and spot welds, not black rubberized spray.', "Rockers, front fender lower rear corners (behind the wheel, ahead of the door), battery tray and adjacent inner fender (acid), floor pans under the seats, spare tire well and the windshield/backlight surrounds under the chrome trim. Trim removal photos are worth more than any seller's statement; chrome-trim rust is a $2,000–$6,000 job with glass out and repaint.", 'M10 iron-block four is robust but the aluminum head cracks between the valve seats, especially 1975–76 US cars fitted with the EGR/thermal-reactor emissions exhaust that cooks the head. Symptoms: chronic coolant loss, combustion gases in the coolant, hot-start hesitation. Head rebuild $1,800–$3,500; complete engine rebuild $6,000–$9,000. Ask for a leakdown/compression test and a block test on the coolant.', 'Timing chain and plastic chain guides/tensioner wear with age; a rattle at cold idle or a chain that has worn a groove in the timing cover is a $700–$1,500 job on the cover, more if the cover is grooved through. Also expect weeping front and rear main seals and a dripping oil-pressure sender.', 'Cooling system is marginal by modern standards: original brass radiator, viscous/fixed fan, water pump and the notorious plastic-impeller failures on replacements, plus a thermostat housing that corrodes. Many good cars have already had an aluminum radiator/electric fan; verify the swap is properly shrouded and wired with a relay, not a toggle switch. Budget $600–$1,200 for radiator/pump/hoses/thermostat if undated.', 'Fuel system: original Solex 32/36 DIDTA carbs are worn out and rarely rebuildable to spec, so Weber 32/36 DGV or 38/38 conversions are near universal. A 38/38 with a hot cam is fun but often jetted rich — check for fuel smell, black plugs, and poor cold idle. Kugelfischer mechanical injection on the tii is the expensive one: pump rebuild $2,000–$3,500, and cold-start/enrichment gremlins are common if the car sits. Original rubber fuel lines and the tank sending unit/tank rust cause leaks and fuel-starvation; verify fuel lines have been replaced (a fire risk on these cars).', 'Ignition: Bosch distributor vacuum advance diaphragms fail (a listed fault on this example), points-era mechanical advance seizes, and 123/Pertronix conversions are common. Symptoms are pinging under load, poor part-throttle economy and weak hot restarts. $150–$450 to correct.', 'Steering and front suspension: the ZF worm-and-roller box develops play, the idler/pitman arms and tie rods wear, and front control-arm bushings and non-serviceable ball joints are consumables. Lowered cars on short springs eat ball joints and cause bump steer. Full front end refresh $1,200–$2,500; a rebuilt steering box is $500–$900 plus install.', 'Driveline: the rubber guibo (flex disc) and driveshaft center support bearing perish and cause launch clunks and a 40–60 mph vibration ($400–$800 done together). The differential mount and rear subframe bushings tear; half-shaft U-joints/CV boots leak.', "Getrag four-speed: second-gear synchro wear (crunch on a cold 1–2 upshift), worn nylon/plastic shift-tower bushings giving vague, rattly shifts, and leaking output and selector-shaft seals. A tower rebuild is cheap; a gearbox rebuild is $1,500–$2,500. Persistent 'weeping' from a gearbox usually means the front or rear seal and often a worn output shaft.", 'Brakes: sin
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid and filter service plus valve lash adjustment (0.006 in cold/0.008 in hot per spec) and a compression/leakdown baseline', 'Distributor service: new vacuum advance, points/condenser or electronic conversion, fresh cap/rotor/wires/plugs, and a timing and carb tune on a gas analyzer', 'Replace all rubber fuel lines from tank to carb, inspect the tank and sending unit for rust, and pressure-check for leaks (fire prevention)', 'Brake hydraulic refresh: flexible hoses, fluid flush, rear wheel cylinder/drum inspection and adjustment, booster and master function check', 'Address gearbox weeping: reseal output/selector shaft seals and rebuild the shift tower bushings if not already done', 'Guibo, driveshaft center support bearing and differential mount inspection and replacement as nee
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Front end refresh: control arm bushings, ball joints, tie rods, idler arm, and an alignment with a corrected ride height', 'Steering box rebuild or adjustment to remove on-center play', 'Clutch hydraulics (master/slave) and, if the pedal is high or the throwout bearing whines, clutch and rear main seal while the box is out', 'Timing chain, guides, tensioner and front cover seal if history is unknown', "Heater box rebuild, blower motor and heater valve — the classic 'do it once with the dash out' job, combined with the cracked-dash replacement", 'Door/window seals, quarter-window seals, trunk and hood seals, and door card clip/regulator work to stop water intrusion', 'Wiring cleanup behind the dash: remove stereo/A/C splices, fuse box and ground refresh, alternator/voltage regulator check
profiles.market_notes: Round-taillight 'roundies' (1968–73) and especially tii cars carry a clear premium over 1974–76 square-taillight cars, and US 1974–76 cars with the big 5-mph 'diving board' bumpers are discounted unless converted to Euro bumpers. Documented, rust-free, honestly presented drivers in desirable period colors (Inka, Malaga, Verona, Agave, Amazon/Taiga green, Colorado, Chamonix) with a sunroof, factory-look interiors and a thick receipt file trade at the top; heavily modified cars with hot cams, big Webers and unknown mileage sell at the low end of the money regardless of cosmetics. Four-speed is the norm and expected; the ZF three-speed automatic is a significant value and desirability penalty. Expect $18k–$35k for good modified drivers, $35k–$60k+ for sorted original-spec roundies and tiis, with restoration receipts and metal-work photos moving price more than paint quality.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 50-year-old car needs its rubber and hydraulics renewed regardless of presentation: fuel lines, brake hoses and fluid, coolant hoses, window/door/trunk seals, motor and subframe mounts, guibo and center bearing, and tires older than six years. Plan a full ignition and carburetion tune plus valve lash and a cooling-system overhaul in the first season, and set aside for the dash-out heater box and cracked dash job that nearly every 02 eventually needs. profiles.label: BMW 135i Convertible (E88, N54 & N55)
profiles.framing: This is the cheap-thrills, short-wheelbase BMW: 300 hp turbo six in a small rear-drive chassis, and in E88 convertible form a genuinely usable top-down daily for Highway 1 and the Monterey Peninsula. For this buyer it is a driver, not an asset — E88 verts sit at the bottom of the 1-Series price ladder while carrying the same running costs as a much more expensive car. The whole exercise is buying maintenance history, not miles: a documented, unmodified, tune-free car with cooling, fuel and turbo work already paid for is worth several thousand dollars more than a cheap one. Salt-free California/Southwest history and a top that has been exercised and drained matter as much as the drivetrain.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Fuel system, N54 cars (2008–2010): the HPFP (high-pressure fuel pump) was the subject of multiple recalls and an extended 10yr/120k warranty that has now expired on every car; symptoms are long cranks, limp mode, 'Half Engine Power' warning, rough cold running. Replacement is roughly $900–1,400. Piezo injectors on N54 failed in waves (index 11/12 supersessions); a full set is $1,500–2,500 installed. 2) N55 cars (2011–2013) use solenoid injectors and a more robust pump but still fail individually — a misfiring cylinder usually means one injector at $250–450 plus labor. 3) Turbocharger wastegate rattle: N54 twin turbos develop wastegate flutter, N55's single twin-scroll turbo develops the same rattle in its electric wastegate actuator, typically past 60–90k miles; audible as a metallic buzz at light throttle 1,500–2,500 rpm and eventually underboost codes. Actuator alone $600–900, turbo replacement $2,500–4,000. 4) Cooling system is consumable, not durable: the electric water pump and thermostat are a 60–90k mile / 8-year item at $900–1,400 together; the plastic expansion tank, coolant hoses and the plastic thermostat housing crack with age. A car with no cooling records at 50k+ miles and 13 years should be assumed to need the whole job. 5) Oil leaks are near-universal by 60–80k: valve cover and VCG gasket ($600–900), oil filter housing gasket ($500–800, contaminates the belt if ignored), and the oil pan gasket ($1,200–1,800 due to subframe clearance). Look for oil on the exhaust manifold and a smell after a hard drive. 6) Direct injection carbon buildup on intake valves: expect walnut blasting every 60–80k miles, $500–900. Symptoms are rough cold idle, misfires under load, mild power loss. 7) The stock plastic charge pipe (both N54 and N55) cracks at the coupler and dumps boost; an aluminum replacement is a sensible, accepted fix — but confirm it accompanied a stock tune, not a boost increase. 8) Tuning/modification is the biggest hidden risk: heavily tuned N54/N55 cars suffer crank hub timing slip, burned pistons, and stretched rod bearings. Any car with a JB4/MHD/Cobb history, upgraded turbos, or a methanol kit should be treated as a rebuild candidate unless the tune history is fully documented and the crank hub pinned. 9) DCT (7-speed GS7D36SG) cars need a mechatronic/clutch fluid service every ~60k miles ($500–800); neglected units show shudder from a stop and eventually mechatronic sleeve leaks or clutch wear — $3,500–6,000 to fix. Manual cars: check clutch and the dual-mass flywheel ($1,500–2,200) and the notorious weak 6-speed synchro feel when cold. 10) Convertible-specific: hydraulic top cylinders and pump leak (fluid on the trunk liner or top well), microswitches/Hall sensors fail and cause the top to stop mid-cycle, and the roll-over bar deployment mechanism can seize. Top mechanism repairs run $800–3,000; a replacement top with glass window is $1,500–2,500 installed. 11) Blocked convertible/cowl drain tubes are the classic cause of wet front footwells and trunk, which then kills body modules and the FRM (footwell module) — a wet-carpet car is a $1,000+ electrical rabbit hole. 12) Suspension and rubber age out: front control arm bushings and rear trailing arm/rear shock mounts around 70–100k ($800–1,500 for a front refresh), plus run-flat-battered wheels and struts. 13) Electrical odds and ends: FRM module failure (windows/lights all dead, coding recovery ~$300–600), Comfort Access door handle sensors, iDrive/CIC screen and CD stereo faults, and the E88 dash leather delaminating around the airbag seam (cosmetic, $500–1,500 to re-wrap). 14) Brakes on M Sport cars use larger rotors and pads that wear fast if driven hard; budget $900–1,400 for a four-corner refresh.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service including engine oil, brake fluid and (if DCT) transmission/mechatronic fluid; new coolant if age is unknown. Replace the cracked/aged plastic charge pipe and boost hoses if still stock. Clear and flush all four convertible/cowl drain tubes and dry/verify the trunk and footwells. Address any known oil weep (valve cover or filter housing gasket) before it fouls the belt. Fresh non-run-flat tires and an alignment; new wiper blades and cabin filter; battery test with registration if replaced. Expect $1,500–3,000 on a decent 50–70k mile car.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Electric water pump and thermostat if not documented ($900–1,400); intake valve walnut blasting ($500–900); one or more fuel injectors ($300–600 each installed); turbo wastegate actuator if rattle is developing ($600–900); front control arm bushings and possibly rear shock mounts ($800–1,500); brake pads/rotors ($900–1,400); convertible top hydraulic seal or microswitch repair ($400–1,200); oil filter housing and/or oil pan gasket ($500–1,800).
profiles.market_notes: Manual coupes (E82) command the strongest money and 135is/6MT cars are the top of the market; DCT convertibles are the value end — typically $3,000–6,000 behind an equivalent manual coupe. N55 cars (2011–2013) generally bring more than N54 for perceived fuel-system reliability, though N54 enthusiasts pay up for unmodified, well-documented examples. Miles matter less than binders: a 70k-mile car with pump/injector/turbo/cooling receipts beats a 45k-mile car with 'no records.' Rare colors like Marrakesh Brown over Terracotta, Le Mans Blue, and Alpine White with M Sport/Sport seats add appeal; heavily tuned, deleted, or accident-history cars are discounted hard and are difficult to resell.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 12–16 year old E88 needs a full age-based catch-up regardless of mileage: coolant system components, all gaskets and rubber hoses, suspension bushings, brake fluid and likely a battery, plus convertible top seals, drains and hydraulics. Low-mileage cars are often worse for rubber and top mechanisms because they have sat. Budget $3,000–5,000 in the first year on top of the purchase price to get a typical example to a trustworthy baseline.

profiles.label: BMW 3 Series E30 (325e/325i/325is, M20 six-cylinder)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the E30 325is is a compact, analog, rear-drive coupe meant to be driven on Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road most weekends — light (2,700 lb), hydraulically steered, with a smooth M20B25 six and a shift linkage that rewards patience. It is not a fast car by modern standards; the appeal is transparency, small footprint, and a parts/knowledge ecosystem that makes long-term ownership realistic. Because these are now 35-40 years old, condition, rust history, and a paper trail matter far more than the odometer reading, and a documented, unmodified, uncracked-dash car with the sport seats and LSD is worth a real premium over a 'clean-looking' unknown. Coastal California living means salt air and damp — a car that has never lived in the Rust Belt is materially more valuable to this buyer than one that spent 30 years in Nebraska or the Northeast.
profiles.weak_points: 1) M20 timing belt and water pump: the M20B25 is an interference engine — a snapped belt bends valves and turns a $400 service into a $3,500-$6,000 head rebuild. Interval is 60k miles or 4-5 years, whichever comes first, and the water pump (early cars used a plastic impeller that disintegrates) and tensioner should go with it. Demand a dated receipt or photo of a chalk-marked belt; if there is no proof, assume it must be done immediately regardless of mileage. 2) Cylinder head cracking between the valve seats on early M20 heads (casting numbers 1277731 and 885) — symptoms are unexplained coolant loss, overheating, or a milky film; a later 1705310 or 1710891 head or a documented replacement is a plus. Head work runs $1,800-$3,500. 3) Cooling system generally: the plastic-neck radiator, expansion tank, thermostat housing, and hoses all become brittle at 25+ years. Any overheating episode on an M20 is a head-gasket/head-crack event waiting to happen. Budget $600-$1,200 for a full cooling refresh. 4) Oil leaks: valve cover gasket, oil filter housing gasket, and the front timing cover/oil pan seams weep on nearly every car; the rear main and oil pan gasket ($700-$1,200 with subframe drop on the pan) are the expensive ones. Check for oil pooling on the exhaust and on the crossmember. 5) Fuel system: the 30+ year old rubber fuel hoses under the car and at the tank, plus the fuel pump and accumulator, are a genuine fire risk on cars with unknown history. Original-looking cracked hoses = replace now, $300-$800. 6) Rust: shock towers (look under the strut mount hats in the engine bay for bubbling or cracking), the battery tray corner in the trunk, the rear subframe/trailing-arm mounting points and floor, rear wheel arches, jack points, sunroof drains and the panel under the rear window seal, and the seam behind the front fenders. A Midwest/Northeast car needs the underside and trunk floor photographed thoroughly. Structural shock-tower or subframe-mount rot is a walk-away or a $3,000+ repair. 7) Interior plastics: cracked dashboard is near-universal ($400-$900 for a good used one plus labor, more for a re-skin), sagging headliner, brittle door cards, failing window regulator clips, and disintegrating sunroof cassette parts. Sport seat bolsters on 325is cars split at the driver's outer bolster; the beige and Cardinal interiors are hardest to source. 8) Suspension and steering bushings: front control arm bushings and ball joints, rear trailing arm bushings (RTABs, cause of vague rear end and inconsistent toe), subframe bushings, sway bar links, and the steering box/center link/idler arm all wear out by 100k. A full front-and-rear refresh with shocks is $1,500-$3,000 installed. Note whether 'shocks replaced' also included struts, mounts, and bump stops or was just dampers. 9) Electrical: the instrument cluster and OBC use failure-prone capacitors and cracked solder joints — dead odometer gears (a black-and-white speedometer needle drift or stuck odo), dim pixel displays in the OBC/SI board, and the SI battery packs that leak onto the board. Cluster odometer gear repair $150-$400. Also check the sunroof motor, central locking pneumatics (early) or actuators, and the notoriously melting relay panel connections. 10) Getrag 260 transmission and driveline: synchros (especially 2nd) start to balk when cold at high miles, the shift linkage bushings and selector rod joint make the shifter sloppy ($100 in parts, big improvement), the giubo/flex disc cracks, the center support bearing collapses (vibration at 45-60 mph), and the guide tube/throwout bearing squeal precedes a clutch job. Clutch/flywheel/rear main combined job runs $1,400-$2,500. 11) Limited-slip differential: the 25% ZF LSD on a 325is wears out and behaves like an open diff; check for one-wheel spin and for gear whine or leaking diff cover/output seals. Diff rebuild or swap $800-$2,000. 12) Brakes and ABS: the ABS control unit and wheel sensors fail, the master cylinder and rear calipe
profiles.immediate_repairs: Timing belt, tensioner, water pump, thermostat, and all coolant hoses unless there is dated proof within 4 years; full fluid service (engine, Getrag 260 with MTL, diff, brake fluid, coolant); replace all rubber fuel lines and check the fuel pump/accumulator; new tires if date codes exceed ~6 years regardless of tread (the Uniroyal Tigerpaws on the example car are a red flag for age); shift linkage bushings and selector rod; flex disc/giubo and center support bearing if there is any driveline vibration; front control arm bushings and ball joints; battery, belts, and a check/clean of the relay panel and grounds.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Rear trailing arm bushings and subframe bushings; rear shock mounts and bump stops; clutch, throwout bearing, guide tube and rear main seal if any squeal or slip; oil filter housing and valve cover gaskets; radiator if still original plastic-neck; instrument cluster odometer gears and SI board battery service; sunroof cassette lubrication and drain clearing; A/C evaluation and likely condenser/dryer/expansion valve refresh; LSD evaluation and possible clutch pack rebuild; dash cap or replacement dash and headliner if sagging; seat bolster repair.
profiles.market_notes: The 325is coupe with 5-speed and factory LSD sits near the top of the non-M E30 hierarchy, above 325i sedans and well above 325e/eta cars; convertibles and 325ix occupy separate niches. Documented low-mileage, unmodified, rust-free cars with original paint, intact uncracked dash, and books/window sticker/records bring the strongest numbers; a Carfax accident, a replaced fender tag, or a repaint drops a car into the driver-grade band. Delphin Gray, Alpine White, Diamond Schwarz and Zinnoberrot are safe; beige/Pearl Beige leather is desirable when clean but expensive to fix when it is not. Modified cars (M50/S52 swaps, coilovers, aftermarket wheels, non-original seats) can be cheaper to buy and are much harder to resell to the documentation-driven auction crowd; typical strong-driver money for a 90k-110k mile 325is is roughly $12k-$20k, with exceptional preserved examples going higher.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 35-40 year old E30 needs a systems catch-up regardless of mileage: every rubber item — coolant hoses, fuel lines, suspension bushings, engine mounts, tires — ages out on the calendar, not the odometer, and low-mileage cars are often worse for seized calipers and dried seals. Budget $3,000-$5,000 in the first year for timing belt/cooling, fuel lines, bushings, and fluid services even on a well-kept car, plus a contingency for the cluster, sunroof, and A/C.

profiles.label: BMW 3 Series E30 Touring (318i / 320i / 325i wagon, grey-market import)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the E30 Touring is a small, honest, analog rear-drive wagon that can actually be used — dog, bikes, Highway 1, weekend hauling — not a garage queen. Every one in the US is a personal or commercial import (the Touring was never federalized), so the paperwork trail and the California registration path matter as much as the mechanicals. A 318i with the M40B18 is the cheapest E30 engine to buy and the most expensive to ignore: it is a belt-driven interference four with a famous camshaft-wear problem, so service documentation outranks a shiny repaint. The realistic goal is a rust-free, documented, mechanically sorted 100–130k-mile example that needs $3–6k of catch-up rather than a cosmetically staged import with a fresh coat of paint over unknown history.
profiles.weak_points: 1) M40B18 camshaft and rocker wear: the M40's cam lobes and hydraulic lifters run marginal oil supply and wear badly if oil changes were stretched — symptoms are ticking that doesn't quiet after warm-up, weak top end, and metallic glitter in the oil filter. A cam, rockers, lifters and head refresh runs $1,800–3,500 installed; a full head is more. Ask for oil-change intervals and any cam/rocker receipt. 2) M40 timing belt: interference engine, belt plus tensioner every 4 years/40–50k miles regardless of miles driven. A snapped belt is bent valves and a $3,000+ job. Demand a dated belt/tensioner/water pump receipt; a faded fuse-box sticker from 2018 is not proof enough on a 2026 car. 3) Cooling system: plastic-neck radiator, plastic-impeller water pump, expansion tank and the thermo-time/temp sensors all fail on age, not miles. Full refresh (radiator, pump, thermostat, hoses, tank, belts) $700–1,200 DIY-parts, $1,500–2,200 shop. Overheating an M40 warps the head. 4) Rust, and this is the make-or-break on a Touring: front shock towers under the strut mounts, jacking points and sills, rear wheel arches, spare-wheel well and rear floor, battery tray, windshield/rear-glass surrounds, sunroof drains, and Touring-specific tailgate lower seam, hatch-glass hinge area and rear cargo floor. Bubbles at the tailgate seam or wet spare well usually mean $2,000–8,000 of real bodywork. A fresh repaint of unknown depth (as in this listing) is a reason to bring a paint gauge and a lift, not a reason to relax. 5) Instrument cluster: the SI-board Ni-Cd batteries leak and destroy the board ($200–500 rebuild), and the odometer gear strips — this is why so many E30s are TMU. A metric cluster on a US-titled car also means every gauge reading and any recorded mileage is a conversion estimate. 6) Suspension bushings and mounts: front control-arm bushings, rear trailing-arm bushings (RTABs), strut and shock mounts, sway-bar links and rear subframe mounts are all consumable at 100k+; a full bushing/mount refresh is $1,200–2,500. Cheap entry-level coilovers (Raceland and similar) commonly ride harshly, leak within a season and often come with wrong spring rates and no corner balancing — budget $1,200–2,000 for OE-height Bilstein/Sachs plus springs to put it back. 7) Steering: E30s use a recirculating-ball box; play at center, a weeping box, and worn idler arm/center link/tie rods are normal at this age. Box $400–900, linkage $300–600. The listing's fresh power-steering pump/reservoir suggests a prior leak — ask what leaked and whether the rack lines and box were addressed. 8) Driveline: guibo (flex disc), center support bearing, driveshaft U-joints and differential mounting bushing all perish; symptoms are a shudder off-throttle and a clunk on shift. $500–1,100 to do properly. 9) Clutch hydraulics and clutch: slave and master cylinders leak with age (a slave was just replaced here — ask whether the master and line went too); clutch job on a 318i $900–1,500. 10) Fuel and idle: Motronic-era idle control valve, crankcase breather hose, fuel pump/filter and 30-year-old rubber fuel lines in the rear — a hard-starting or hunting idle is usually ICV or vacuum leaks. Rear fuel-line replacement is cheap parts, fire risk if ignored. 11) Interior aging: cracked dash top, sagging headliner (Touring headliners are large, $400–800 retrim), brittle door-card vinyl, failing window regulators, sticky switchgear and dead cargo-cover mechanisms. Touring-specific trim and cargo pieces are hard to source in the US. 12) Touring-specific electrics: the tailgate wiring loom runs through rubber conduit at the hinge and chafes/breaks — dead rear wiper, dead rear defrost, or dead hatch lock; repair is tedious but cheap. Rear wiper motors and the separately-opening glass hinges seize and corrode. 13) Rear self-leveling: some European Tourings carry Nivomat-type self-leveling rear dampers; failed units sag and replacement is expensive, and cars converted to conventional shocks may stil
profiles.immediate_repairs: Timing belt, tensioner, water pump, thermostat and accessory belts unless there is a dated receipt inside 4 years/40k miles; full cooling-system refresh including radiator, hoses and expansion tank; fresh oil with a filter cut-open inspection for cam debris; four tires (2016/2018 date codes are hard-expired and dangerous); brake fluid flush, pads/rotors and a rear caliper check; clutch master cylinder and line if only the slave was replaced; fuel filter and inspection/replacement of rear rubber fuel lines; ICV clean and vacuum-hose replacement; headlight/turn-signal and taillight function check for US road legality; and the California registration/BAR referee process — budget time and fees, and be ready to revert Euro lighting.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Replace the budget coilovers with OE-height Bilstein/Sachs and correct springs, plus new strut/shock mounts and bearings; front control arms and bushings, RTABs, sway-bar links, tie rods and idler arm/center link; steering box or box rebuild if play persists; guibo, center support bearing and differential mount; instrument cluster SI-board battery removal/rebuild and odometer gear; headliner retrim and driver's seat/door-card repair; sunroof drain cleaning and reseal; A/C system evaluation (R12-era system, likely needs conversion or delete); exhaust hangers and possibly a rear muffler section; and a paint-depth-guided investigation plus repair of any rust found at the tailgate seam, jacking points or shock towers.
profiles.market_notes: Six-cylinder Tourings (325i, and especially 325iX all-wheel drive) trade at a clear premium over the four-cylinder 318i, and manuals over automatics; within 318i cars the earlier M40 and later M43 are similar money. Documented, unmolested, original-paint imports with a clean import file and a straightforward registration path bring the most; fresh repaints, TMU metric clusters, budget coilovers and replica M-Tech II kits suppress value with knowledgeable buyers even when they attract auction bidders. Desirable colors (Alpine White, Lachs Silber, Diamantschwarz, and period blues) and factory options like a sunroof, sport seats and the rear cargo cover help; a $18–22k result for a modified 318i Touring is essentially paying a rarity/novelty premium, since a similar-money 325i sedan or coupe is far better sorted. Records matter more than mileage on these — a 150k-mile car with a folder beats a 100k TMU car with a shine.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 35-year-old import needs a full fluids/rubber/cooling reset regardless of what the ad says: belts, hoses, radiator, pump, fuel lines, brake and clutch hydraulics, tires, and all suspension bushings and mounts. On a modified example add reversing cheap coilovers to OE-height quality dampers and correcting anything the body kit installation disturbed. Budget $4,000–6,000 of catch-up in year one on a good car and treat the import/registration process as a separate project with its own timeline.

profiles.label: BMW 3 Series Touring (E91 328i / 328xi Wagon)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the E91 is the classic do-everything answer: a normally aspirated inline-six wagon with a real manual option, hatch practicality for Monterey Peninsula weekends, and enough chassis feel to make Highway 1 and Laureles Grade worth driving. It is a $10k–$25k car with $60k-car maintenance costs, so the value case lives or dies on records: cooling system, VANOS, gaskets, suspension, and (on autos) transmission fluid. Because it is a driver, not an investment, condition and documented catch-up work matter more than mileage. In California the emissions story is decisive — SULEV N51 cars, engine swaps, and deleted/tuned hardware all interact with biennial smog and BAR rules.
profiles.weak_points: Cooling system is the signature E9x expense: the electric water pump and its associated thermostat are effectively a 60–90k-mile wear item, and failure is often abrupt (limp mode, overheat warning). Budget $900–$1,400 installed for pump plus thermostat; ask for a dated invoice, not 'recently done.' The plastic coolant expansion tank, upper/lower hose necks, and radiator end tanks go brittle by 10–12 years and weep or split; a full refresh is $600–$1,200. The N52's magnesium-alloy block is durable but leaks: the valve cover (plastic, warps) and its gasket, the oil filter housing gasket, and the oil pan gasket are near-universal by 90–130k. Valve cover $500–$900; oil filter housing gasket $500–$900 and important because oil drips onto the serpentine belt — a shredded belt can be pulled into the front crank seal and cause catastrophic damage. VANOS solenoids and the VANOS bolts/exhaust adjustment unit cause rough cold idle, a 2A87/2A82 code and lazy throttle; solenoids are cheap, a full VANOS unit is $800–$1,500. The DISA intake flap valve can shed its plastic pivot into the intake — $250–$400 to replace, cheap insurance. Valve stem seals are the classic N51/N52 sin: a puff of blue smoke on cold start or after long idle, especially on California SULEV N51 cars, and a head-off-optional-but-expensive job at $2,000–$3,500. Watch smog readiness monitors and NOx-related codes on N51 cars. Wagon-specific: the tailgate glass hinges crack and the rear hatch wiring loom chafes inside its rubber boot, causing dead wiper, dead lock, dead lights and intermittent tailgate release; hinges $400–$900, loom repair $200–$500. Rear light cluster and hatch seals leak into the spare-wheel well — pull the trunk floor and look for standing water, rust, and a corroded battery cable or amplifier if so equipped. Panoramic roof cassettes are heavy and troublesome: blocked drains dump water into the headliner and A/B-pillar carpets, and the cassette slide/cable can fail ($1,000–$2,500). Suspension bushings are consumables: front control arm/thrust arm bushings, rear trailing arm bushings and rear shock mounts all knock and wander by 80–120k; a full front and rear refresh is $1,200–$2,500. Rear wheel bearings and front hub bearings hum by 100k, $400–$700 each corner. Electrics: the FRM footwell module can brick during a low-voltage jump or battery swap, taking out lights and windows ($300–$800 to repair/recode); the FSU/blower final stage resistor kills fan speeds; and the battery must be registered when replaced or charging strategy cooks the new one. On manuals, the shift shaft seal leaks gear oil onto the underbody, the clutch delay valve is commonly deleted, and clutch plus dual-mass flywheel is $1,800–$3,000. On the 6HP19 automatic, the 'lifetime' fluid is not — unserviced units at 120k+ show flare and harsh 2-3 shifts; fluid and pan/filter service is $500–$800 and the mechatronic sleeve/adapter leak is a common $600–$1,200 job. Finally, run-flat tires and 18-inch wheels crack rims and beat the bushings; check for bent/repaired wheels and consider non-runflats.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Oil service with a real BMW-spec 5W-30, coolant condition test and expansion tank/hose inspection, full fault-code scan with freeze-frame, battery test and registration if replaced, serpentine belt and pulleys if any oil-filter-housing weep is present, DISA valve inspection, sunroof drain flush, tailgate loom and hinge inspection, alignment plus four matched tires if staggered/mismatched, and rear brake pads/rotors (BMW pads wear rears first).
profiles.repairs_12mo: Electric water pump and thermostat if not documented within 60k miles, valve cover gasket and oil filter housing gasket, front control arm bushings and possibly rear shock mounts/trailing arm bushings, VANOS solenoid cleaning or replacement, automatic transmission fluid and pan/filter (or manual shift shaft seal), one or two wheel bearings, expansion tank and radiator hoses, and window regulator or FSU blower resistor as they surface.
profiles.market_notes: Manual-transmission 328i wagons are the enthusiast currency here and carry a meaningful premium over slushbox cars — a clean documented 6-speed can bring double an equivalent automatic. Sport package with the proper seats, xDrive (valued in snow markets, less so in Carmel), Montego Blue/Space Gray/Alpine White over saddle or black, and non-panoramic roofs all help; heavy modification, engine swaps, salvage history, and 150k+ miles compress value fast. Records are worth more than mileage: a 130k car with a folder of cooling, VANOS and suspension invoices should outbid a 90k car with no history. Cars with California-legal emissions status (stock N51/N52 with intact CARB-legal hardware) are worth a clear premium locally because a swapped or tuned car may be unregisterable without a BAR referee sticker.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 110–140k-mile E91 is due for a cooling-system refresh, the standard trio of oil leaks (valve cover, filter housing, pan), and a round of front and rear bushings — plan $3,000–$5,000 of deferred catch-up in the first year unless invoices prove otherwise. Rubber and plastic are the real age items on a 13–18 year old car: hoses, mounts, sunroof drains, hatch loom, and window regulators. Buying the car with the thickest documented folder is cheaper than buying the lowest-mileage example.

profiles.label: BMW 335is (E92 Coupe / E93 Convertible, N54)
profiles.framing: The 335is is the send-off N54 car: 320 hp / 370 lb-ft on overboost, upgraded cooling, M Sport suspension and seats, offered only as a coupe or retractable-hardtop convertible with a 6-speed manual or 7-speed DCT. For this buyer it is an enthusiast bridge car — a fast, analog-feeling, daily-usable GT that is cheap to buy and expensive to neglect. What matters most is a documented, never-tuned N54 with paper on the high-pressure fuel pump, injectors, turbo wastegates and cooling system, and (on the E93) a hardtop that cycles perfectly with dry drain paths. A sorted example is a genuine driver; a deferred-maintenance example will hand back the purchase discount within a year.
profiles.weak_points: 1) HIGH-PRESSURE FUEL PUMP (N54 HPFP, Bosch): the signature failure. Symptoms are long crank, rough cold idle, limp mode and codes 29E1/29E2/29F1/30FF. BMW's extended coverage (10yr/120k) has expired on all of these cars. Expect $900–$1,400 installed; want a receipt showing the latest index part number. 2) PIEZO FUEL INJECTORS: index 11/12 injectors leak and cause misfires, rough cold start, fuel smell and washed-down cylinders. Replacement is $180–300 each plus labor — a full set with decoupling elements and labor is $1,800–2,800. Ask which index is installed and when. 3) TURBO WASTEGATE RATTLE: the twin small turbos develop wastegate flapper/bushing wear — a diesel-like rattle at 1,200–2,000 rpm and, later, underboost codes (30FF, 2B2A/2B2B, boost deviation) and limp mode. Rebuilt or new turbos run $2,500–4,500 installed; this is the single biggest budget item on a high-mile or tuned car. 4) CARBON BUILD-UP ON INTAKE VALVES: direct injection with no port wash; misfires, rough idle and lost power by 50–70k miles. Walnut blasting is $500–900 and is due roughly every 40–60k. Low-mileage but old cars still coke up from short trips. 5) CHARGE PIPE / BOOST PLUMBING: the OEM plastic charge pipe and the boost solenoid o-rings crack, usually announced by a pop and sudden limp mode; $250–600 to fix with an aluminum pipe. Any tuned car is far more likely to have already blown one. 6) COOLING SYSTEM: electric water pump and thermostat are wear items at roughly 60–90k miles or 8–10 years ($1,100–1,700 for the pair installed); the 335is also carries extra radiators/oil cooler, and the plastic expansion tank, radiator neck and coolant hoses go brittle with age. The radiator fan module (as replaced on the example car) is a known failure. 7) OIL LEAKS: valve cover and valve cover gasket (the cover itself cracks and the integrated CCV/PCV fails — $700–1,200), oil filter housing gasket ($500–900), and oil pan gasket ($800–1,500 because the subframe drops). Look for oil on the exhaust manifold/turbo area and a burning smell. 8) VANOS / SOLENOIDS AND ELECTRIC WATER PUMP-ADJACENT ELECTRICS: VANOS solenoid rattle codes (2A82/2A87), and an aged main battery that must be properly registered — an unregistered battery slowly cooks the alternator/IBS system. 9) E93 RETRACTABLE HARDTOP: hydraulic pump and cylinders leak into the trunk, microswitches and the CTM throw "top inoperative" errors, and the trunk partition must be latched. A full top repair is $1,200–3,500; hydraulic cylinder resealing alone is ~$1,500. 10) WATER INTRUSION: clogged roof and cowl drains dump water into the footwells and under the seats, where the junction box, seat modules and airbag sensors live. Damp carpet, musty smell or corroded connectors is a walk-away-level problem. 11) DCT (GS7D36SG) SERVICE: fluid and filter every ~50k miles or 5 years ($600–900); neglected units get harsh low-speed engagement and eventually mechatronic/clutch faults ($3,000+). Manual cars need clutch and slave/master cylinder attention around 70–100k. 12) SUSPENSION AND RUBBER: front control-arm bushings and rear trailing-arm/guide-rod bushings wear by 60–80k ($700–1,400), and the M Sport shocks are typically tired by 90k. Run-flat 19s beat up the chassis and the wheels bend on potholes. 13) TUNED-CAR RISK: a flashed or JB4 car raises the odds of sheared crank hub (crank timing slip, catastrophic), grenaded turbos, cracked charge pipe and stretched rod bolts. Absence of a tune history — and an ECU read showing stock calibration — is worth real money. 14) LOW-MILEAGE-CAR RISK: cars like the example (11k miles, 14 years old) have age-failed rubber and seals — tires with old date codes, dry-rotted coolant hoses, hardened top seals, stale brake and DCT fluid, and fuel system parts that fail shortly after being woken up.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid catch-up: engine oil with OEM filter, brake fluid flush, DCT fluid/filter or manual gearbox oil, coolant condition test. Tires if date codes are over 6 years regardless of tread, plus alignment. Battery test and proper registration/coding if replaced. Cooling system pressure test with replacement of any brittle hose, expansion tank or the radiator fan module. Walnut-blast the intake valves if there is no record within 40k miles. Replace the plastic charge pipe with an aluminum unit and refresh the boost-solenoid o-rings. Diagnose and fix any oil weep at the valve cover or oil filter housing. On an E93: clear and flush all four roof/cowl drains, cycle the top 10+ times, inspect the trunk for hydraulic fluid. Full ISTA/INPA fault-memory read and clear, then re-drive.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Expect one or more of: HPFP replacement if not already documented ($900–1,400); an injector or a matched set with decoupling elements ($400–2,800); water pump and thermostat if original or over ~8 years ($1,100–1,700); valve cover/gasket and oil filter housing gasket ($1,200–2,000 combined); front control-arm and rear guide-rod bushings ($700–1,400); spark plugs and coils on a 40k/5-year interval ($400–700); and, on a car that already rattles, turbo wastegate repair or replacement ($2,500–4,500). E93 owners should budget for hydraulic cylinder reseal or a top microswitch/sensor over the first year or two.
profiles.market_notes: The 335is carries a clear premium over a same-year 335i and is the most desirable non-M N54 E9x; 6-speed manual coupes bring the strongest money and the DCT convertible the softest, with the E93's extra weight and top complexity knocking value relative to the coupe. Documented, never-tuned cars with HPFP/injector/turbo receipts and a clean Carfax sell for real premiums over cheap, boosted, tuned examples — the spread between a sorted car and a project is often larger than the price of the repairs. Low-mileage time-capsule cars (under 25k) command collector-adjacent asks but must be discounted for age-related catch-up and multi-year Carfax service gaps; strong colors (Alpine White, Space Grey, Le Mans Blue, Black Sapphire) with Coral Red or Oyster interiors and the correct 19-inch Style 225 wheels help, while worn/repainted panels, aftermarket exhausts/intakes and missing keys hurt.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2011–2013 335is is now 12–15 years old, so age — not mileage — drives the first bills: brittle coolant hoses and expansion tank, hardened top and window seals, aged tires and brake fluid, and a fuel system that often fails shortly after a long-stored car is put back into service. Budget $2,500–4,000 in the first six months for fluids, cooling refresh, tires, carbon service and a charge-pipe/boost-plumbing update even on a low-mileage, well-presented example, and treat the HPFP/injectors and wastegates as scheduled expenses rather than surprises.

profiles.label: BMW M3 (E46, S54)
profiles.framing: This is the last naturally aspirated, hydraulically steered M3 — a 8,000-rpm S54 with a real 6-speed and a chassis that rewards a canyon run over Highway 1 or Laureles Grade far more than it rewards a spreadsheet. For a Carmel driver this is a weekend-plus-occasional-commute car: coastal salt air is mild, but marine damp punishes soft tops, subframe seam sealer, and neglected cooling systems. What matters most is documentation of the four expensive E46 M3 stories — rod bearings, rear subframe mounts, VANOS, and cooling system — because a cheap car with none of those records is not cheap. The convertible is heavier, softer, and worth meaningfully less than a coupe, so it should be bought as a driver, never as an appreciation play.
profiles.weak_points: Rear subframe mounting point cracking is the defining E46 M3 flaw: the four floor-pan mounting points and the surrounding sheet metal tear away from the trunk floor, most commonly on cars over ~60k miles, with harder-driven and clutch-dumped cars failing earlier. Symptoms are a clunk on throttle transitions, cracked seam sealer visible under the trunk carpet and above the differential, and in bad cases a visibly deformed floor. Proper repair is a reinforcement plate kit (CMP, Redish, Vorshlag) welded in — $2,500–$5,000 done right; look for photos of the weld-in job, not just "seam sealer looked fine." Rod bearings are the headline engine risk: BMW's original spec left marginal clearance, and while catastrophic failure is less common than internet lore suggests, prophylactic replacement with new-spec (or aftermarket ACL/King) bearings and new rod bolts is a $1,500–$3,000 job, done in-car. Ask for a receipt with the date, mileage, part numbers, and ideally a Blackstone oil analysis showing low lead/copper; an unknown-history 90k car with no bearing history should be priced with that job assumed. VANOS is a wear item, not a maybe: the exhaust hub bolts can back out, the intake/exhaust solenoid pack seals harden, and the high-pressure oil line rots — symptoms are a rattle at idle, loss of low-end torque, and codes for VANOS position. Beisan seal/rattle-fix kits and hub reseal run $800–$2,000 with labor; the earlier-recall single VANOS hub was addressed by BMW on many 2001–2003 cars, but verify. Cooling system is a full-replacement item every 60–80k miles or 8–10 years: plastic-impeller water pump, thermostat, expansion tank, radiator, hoses, and the notorious plastic thermostat-housing/coolant necks — $1,200–$2,000 as a package. The listing example shows a 2022 pump/thermostat at 78k, which covers the two biggest pieces but not necessarily the radiator or expansion tank. SMG II cars add a hydraulic pump ($1,500–$2,500), accumulator, and clutch position sensor to the risk list; manuals are strongly preferred and command more money. Clutch and dual-mass flywheel typically go together at 80k–120k for $2,000–$3,000; a chattering pedal-up rattle or shudder on take-up is the tell. Valve adjustment is a genuine S54 maintenance item every 30k miles or so ($600–$1,000 with shims) and is very often skipped — ask for it by name; a car with no valve adjustment record in 60k miles is a red flag on overall care. Oil consumption of a quart per 1,500–2,000 miles is normal-ish; more than that with blue smoke on overrun points at valve stem seals or worse. The CDV, rear shock mounts, front control arm bushings (FCAB), and rear trailing arm bushings are all $600–$1,500 suspension refresh items that most 20-plus-year-old cars need, and worn RTABs mimic subframe clunk. Convertibles add their own list: the power soft-top hydraulic cylinders and pump leak fluid onto the trunk carpet, the top's rear window and seams shrink and leak, the roll-over bar deployment system and its microswitches misbehave, and the tonneau/flap motors are expensive one-off parts — budget $1,500–$4,000 for a top replacement plus mechanism repairs. Electrical gremlins are routine: pixel loss in the instrument cluster and OBC ($200–$400 to repair), failing final stage resistor for the blower, a dying cluster stepper motor, sticky interior trim/soft-touch coating, and a glovebox latch that only works with the key (as noted in this listing) is a classic worn-latch item. Finally, the front control arm/steering rack bushing wear plus 20-year-old rubber engine and trans mounts make the car feel vague — cheap individually, but they add up fast.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service (oil with the correct 10W-60 or a quality modern equivalent, brake, clutch, diff with LSD additive) if not documented within a year; front brake pads and likely rotors as flagged by the seller's technician ($600–$900); the cracked A/C belt plus serpentine belt, tensioners and pulleys ($400–$700); a proper subframe inspection with the trunk carpet and rear undertrays removed, and immediate scheduling of reinforcement if any cracking is found; battery registration and confirmation of the recently installed battery; VANOS rattle assessment and Beisan seal kit if the idle rattle is present; convertible top hydraulic leak check and soft-top seal/hinge lubrication; valve clearance check if there is no record within 30k miles.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Rod bearing and rod bolt replacement if there is no documented prior service (budget $2,000–$3,000 and treat it as scheduled, not optional, at 90k with a history gap); completion of the cooling system — radiator, expansion tank, upper/lower hoses, coolant necks — since only the pump and thermostat are documented; clutch and dual-mass flywheel if any shudder or high engagement point is noted ($2,000–$3,000); front control arm bushings, rear trailing arm bushings, rear shock mounts and possibly all four dampers ($1,200–$2,500); soft-top replacement or rear-window repair if the material is shrunken or the seams are separating ($1,200–$2,500); instrument cluster pixel repair; new tires if the current set is over six years old regardless of tread; interior refresh items — driver's bolster reuph
profiles.market_notes: Coupes command a clear premium over convertibles — often 25–40% for equivalent condition — and 6-speed manuals are worth substantially more than SMG cars, with an SMG-to-manual swap history usually a net negative unless fully documented. The Competition Package (ZCP, 2005–2006, with 19-inch CSL-style wheels, quicker rack, and cross-drilled rotors) and Laguna Seca Blue, Phoenix Yellow, and Imola Red over Cinnamon or Kiwi carry the strongest desirability; black over black is the most common and least differentiated combination. Documented rod bearings, a welded subframe reinforcement, a recent cooling system, and a valve adjustment history can swing a car by $6,000–$10,000 against an unknown-history equivalent, which is exactly the value of paperwork on this model. Mileage matters less than records below about 120k, but Carfax gaps, rust-belt titles, and salvage/branded history all cut hard.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 20-plus-year-old S54 needs a systematic catch-up regardless of mileage: all rubber cooling components, belts and pulleys, suspension bushings, engine and transmission mounts, and every fluid on a documented interval. On this specific convertible, add the soft-top hydraulics and fabric to that list, and treat rod bearings and the remaining cooling components as scheduled work rather than contingencies given the ownership gap and the 2012-purchase, low-annual-mileage storage pattern.

profiles.label: BMW Z3 Coupe (E36/8, incl. M Coupe)
profiles.framing: The 'clown shoe' is a short-wheelbase, stiff-shell hatchback built on E36 Z3 running gear — a genuinely rare, characterful weekend and back-road car for Carmel/Highway 1 and Laureles Grade duty, not a commuter. For this buyer it is an enthusiast bridge car: manual, unmodified, documented, and bought on chassis integrity rather than on shine. Values now split sharply between the S52/S54 M Coupe and the 2.8/3.0i coupe, so verifying exactly which car is in front of you is step one. Because the E36/8 has a known structural weak point (rear subframe mounting area), evidence of a clean underbody inspection outranks cosmetics, mileage, or 'like new' claims.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Rear subframe mounting points: the trunk floor sheetmetal where the rear subframe bolts up can crack, tear, or deform — the single most important E36/8 issue, disproportionately on M Coupes and any car driven hard or on sticky tires/lowered stiff suspension. Symptoms are hairline cracks radiating from the four mount cups, paint flaking, sealant splitting, or a 'clunk/wander' under load. Reinforcement plates (Redish, Vincebar, or BMW dealer plates) welded in run $2,000–$4,000; repairing already-torn metal $4,000–$7,000+. Look for photos of the trunk floor with carpet and spare tire out, and receipts naming the shop and plate kit. 2) Cooling system (M52TU 2.8 and M54 3.0i): plastic-necked radiator, expansion tank, thermostat housing, and water pump with plastic impeller are all life-limited at 60–100k miles or ~10–12 years, whichever comes first — regardless of odometer, a 25-year-old car on original cooling parts is a roadside failure waiting to happen. Full refresh $900–$1,800. A cooked M52TU/M54 head from an overheat is a $4,000+ event. 3) VANOS: rattle at idle/light throttle, lazy low-end torque; seal kit (Beisan) $200 DIY, $700–$1,200 at a shop. S54 M Coupes have the more complex, more expensive double-VANOS. 4) S54 rod bearings (2001–2002 M Coupe only): the well-known interval item; without a documented bearing service (~$2,000–$3,500 with rod bolts and oil analysis), assume it's due. Also check for the BMW VANOS/rod-bearing recall history and oil-pump nut/shaft. 5) Oil leaks: valve cover gasket, oil filter housing gasket, and oil pan gasket all weep by 80–120k miles; $400–$1,200 each depending on access. Look for oil on the exhaust manifold and burning smell. 6) Crankcase ventilation (CCV/oil separator) on M54 3.0i and M52TU: clogged separator causes smoke, rough idle, and can pull the dipstick out; $400–$800. 7) Driveline mounts and bushings: rear differential bushings and diff mount, driveshaft flex disc (guibo) and center support bearing, and rear trailing arm bushings all age out and cause clunks and driveline shudder; $800–$2,000 to do the set. Original diff-mount failures also contribute to subframe stress. 8) Rear hatch and glass sealing: the coupe leaks into the spare-tire well through the hatch seal, third brake light, and taillight gaskets — pull the trunk carpet and look for staining, rust, or a musty smell; the water also feeds subframe corrosion. Hatch struts sag ($100). 9) Interior electrics/trim: instrument cluster pixel loss (cluster rebuild $150–$350), sticky soft-touch coating on console/vents, sagging headliner, window regulator clips, and glovebox/ashtray plastics. Parts for coupe-specific trim (rear side glass, hatch, cargo cover, rear panels) are scarce and expensive. 10) ABS/ASC module and wheel-speed sensors: dashboard triangle plus ABS light; module rebuild $250–$500, sensors $100 each. 11) Secondary air pump and DISA valve (M54): CEL codes P0491/P0492 and a rattling DISA flap; $250–$600. 12) Clutch and hydraulics: clutch typically 100–140k miles; slave/master cylinders leak with age. Clutch job $1,400–$2,200 due to transmission removal. 13) Suspension bushings and shocks: front control arm bushings, rear shock mounts (RSMs) and their reinforcement, and 25-year-old dampers — a full refresh with quality parts is $1,500–$2,500. Many coupes have been lowered on coilovers with big wheels, which accelerates subframe and RSM damage. 14) Rust: California cars are usually clean, but East Coast/Midwest examples rot at the rear fender arches, rockers, jack points, trunk floor seams, and the subframe area itself — this is a specific problem for the listed New York car. Bushing replacement is not evidence of structural soundness; the trunk-floor welds and differential mounting area are a separate inspection and a separate repair (https://www.autoengineering.com/portfolio/bmw-z3-rear-subframe-mounting-points-repair/).
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full underbody/trunk-floor inspection with the carpet and spare out, and reinforcement plates if any cracking is found ($2,000–$4,000). Complete cooling-system refresh if not documented within 8 years/60k miles (radiator, expansion tank, thermostat, hoses, water pump) $900–$1,800. All fluids including differential and manual gearbox, plus brake fluid flush ($400–$700). New tires if the 19s are period no-name rubber, and ideally a return to a correct-offset 17-inch M Coupe/OEM-style wheel and OE-spec suspension ($1,500–$3,000). Reseal the hatch/taillight gaskets and clear the trunk drains ($200–$500). Battery, wipers, and a full pre-drive brake inspection.
profiles.repairs_12mo: VANOS seal kit and DISA/CCV service ($700–$1,500). Valve cover and oil filter housing gaskets ($700–$1,400). Guibo, center support bearing, diff and trailing arm bushings ($1,000–$2,000). Shocks and rear shock mounts if not recently done ($1,200–$2,000). Cluster pixel repair and window regulator clips ($300–$600). On a 2001–02 S54 car, budget rod bearings and a valve adjustment ($2,500–$4,000). Clutch and hydraulics if the pedal is high or shudders ($1,600–$2,200).
profiles.market_notes: The market is bimodal: S52/S54 M Coupes are collector cars ($45k–$100k+ depending on year, color, and records), while 2.8/3.0i coupes are enthusiast cars typically $18k–$32k, with the 2001–02 3.0i manual at the top. Documented subframe reinforcement, a rust-free Western car, factory wheels, and a thick service file add real money; lowered coilovers, 19-inch wheels, aftermarket exhaust, and repainted or Bondo'd rear arches subtract it. Rare factory colors (Imola Red, Estoril Blue, Titanium Silver, Hell Red) and clean two-tone leather help; black-on-black with modifications is the commodity spec. Automatic 2.8 coupes trade at a meaningful discount and are hard to resell; low mileage without records is worth far less than average mileage with them.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 25-year-old, low-mileage example needs age-based rather than mileage-based work: every cooling component, all rubber (hoses, bushings, guibo, motor and trans mounts), fuel lines, brake fluid and possibly calipers, tires regardless of tread, and seals that have dried out from sitting. Budget $3,000–$5,000 in the first year on a nice non-M coupe just to make it a trustworthy Highway 1 driver, plus the subframe reinforcement if not already done.

profiles.label: BMW Z3 Roadster & Coupe (E36/7, E36/8)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the Z3 is a cheap-to-buy, analog, rear-drive weekend roadster for Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road — hydraulic steering, a real handbrake, an inline-six, and a top that drops in fifteen seconds. A 2002 is the last and best year: M54 2.5i/3.0i engines, updated interior, and the wide rear track. It is emphatically not an investment car (M Roadster/M Coupe excepted), so buy the best-documented, unmolested six-cylinder manual you can find and treat the purchase price as the smaller half of the equation. Coastal fog, salt air, and a 20+ year old convertible top mean condition and storage history matter more here than mileage.
profiles.weak_points: Rear subframe mounting points: the single most important Z3 issue. The floor pan sheet metal around the four differential/subframe mounts tears and cracks, especially on 2.8/3.0i/M cars and any car that saw autocross, hard launches, or a heavy tow hitch. It is often invisible until you pull the trunk carpet and spare and inspect the sheet metal from above, or get under the car and look at the seams around the mounts. Repair is a welded reinforcement kit (Turner/Redish Motorsport/AKG plates) at roughly $2,000–$4,500 depending on how far the tears have propagated; ignoring it eventually means a floor pan section. Ask for photos of bare metal at all four mounts. Cooling system: M52TU/M54 cooling parts are plastic and time-expired at 20 years — radiator end tanks, expansion tank, thermostat housing, water pump (plastic impeller on some), and the radiator neck all fail without warning and an overheat can warp the aluminum head ($3,000+). A full cooling refresh is $700–$1,200 in parts and should be treated as a maintenance interval, not a repair; look for receipts within the last 8 years/60k miles. VANOS: M52TU/M54 single/double VANOS uses O-rings and seals that harden, producing a diesel-like rattle at idle, weak low-end torque, and rough cold running; seal kits are $150 in parts, $600–$900 installed, and a rebuilt unit is $1,000+. Crankcase ventilation (CCV/oil separator): the M54's CCV diaphragm and heater hoses crack, causing high crankcase vacuum, whistling, oil consumption, sucked-out rear main seal, and rough idle; $400–$700 to do properly with all the hoses. Oil filter housing gasket and valve cover gasket: near-universal leaks by 100k, oil drips onto the exhaust manifold and makes the classic BMW hot-oil smell; $300–$600 each. DISA valve (M54): the intake manifold flap pivot fails and can shed plastic into the engine; rebuild kit or replacement, $150–$350. Convertible top: the rear plastic window yellows, cracks and separates from the fabric; the top itself shrinks and the frame pivots seize. A quality Haartz cloth top with glass window installed is $1,200–$2,000, and a torn rear window on a coastal car means a wet interior and a rusting floor. Check the drain channels behind the seats. Rust and water intrusion: inspect rocker panels below the doors, the rear wheel arch lips, the seams under the sill trim, the trunk floor/spare well, and the battery tray (battery lives in the trunk on the passenger side); trunk lid seal and taillight gaskets leak and quietly rot the trunk pan. Electrical/interior: instrument cluster and OBC LCD pixel loss (a $150–$250 refurb), failing door lock actuators/microswitches, window regulators, and the notorious brittle interior trim; the headliner in the Coupe sags. Seats: driver's seat bolster and base foam collapse, and the seat frame bushings squeak; a re-foam and reupholster is $600–$1,200. Suspension/steering: front control arm (thrust arm) bushings and tie rods are 60–80k-mile items that cause shimmy under braking; rear shock mounts crack; original dampers on any surviving example are long dead. Budget $1,200–$2,000 for a full front-end and damper refresh. Driveline: hydraulic clutch master/slave cylinders weep and leave a soft pedal ($300–$500); the rear differential bushing and the driveshaft center support bearing/flex disc (guibo) fail with vibration at 60–80 mph ($500–$900). Fuel: level sender and in-tank pump failures give erratic gauge readings and hot-start issues. Secondary air pump and its check valve fail and throw P0491/P0492 codes that will block a smog pass — plan $400–$700. Finally, the 1.9L four (M44) is slow, weaker in resale, and shares the timing chain guide and cooling issues without the six's charm; a four-cylinder 2002 does not exist in the US, so a 2002 will be a 2.5i, 3.0i, or M.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full cooling system refresh (radiator, expansion tank, thermostat, water pump, hoses, cap) unless documented recent; oil service with a proper BMW filter; CCV/oil separator and hose set on the M54; oil filter housing and valve cover gaskets if seeping; convertible top rear window or full top if cracked/hazed plus clearing the top-well drains; four matching date-coded tires (age-outs are common on low-mile cars); front control arm bushings and tie rods if there is any shimmy; battery and trunk battery-tray cleanup; brake fluid flush.
profiles.repairs_12mo: VANOS seal service if the rattle is present; DISA valve rebuild; shocks/struts and rear shock mounts; clutch hydraulics; driveshaft flex disc, center support bearing and differential bushing; secondary air pump/valve if a smog code appears; instrument cluster pixel repair; door lock actuators and window regulator; seat foam/bolster repair; soft-top frame pivot service and re-lube; exhaust flex section or rear muffler; subframe reinforcement plates preemptively if the car is a 3.0i/M and shows early stress marks.
profiles.market_notes: Six-cylinder manuals carry the market: a documented 2002 3.0i manual with a hardtop, sport package and clean floors is the top of the non-M range, while automatics and the 2.5i sell noticeably softer. M Roadster and especially M Coupe live in a separate, much higher tier and demand S54 rod-bearing and subframe evidence. A factory hardtop adds $1,500–$2,500, and desirable colors (Steel Blue, Topaz Blue, Imola/Hell Red, Titanium Silver) with a contrasting or well-preserved interior move cars fast; grey/black on black with a tired top is the discount end. Records and rust-free southwestern/coastal-garaged provenance are worth more than a low odometer, and mileage below 60k mostly matters for the cosmetics it implies.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2002 Z3 is a 20+ year old car whose rubber, plastic, and fabric are all time-expired regardless of mileage: expect to spend $3,000–$5,000 in the first year on cooling system, CCV, gaskets, suspension bushings, dampers, tires, and likely the convertible top. None of it is exotic and most is DIY-friendly, but budgeting for it up front is the difference between a delightful cheap roadster and a rolling disappointment.

profiles.label: Ford Bronco (First Generation, 1966–1977 "Early Bronco")
profiles.framing: For this buyer the early Bronco is a weekend-and-errand toy that has to actually drive to Big Sur, Laureles Grade, and the beach without drama — not a trailer queen and not a show car. Because almost none survive unmodified, the realistic goal is a documented, coherently built truck: rust-free structure, one shop's fingerprints on the driveline, and receipts that explain every deviation from stock. The single biggest determinant of long-term cost is metal — body mounts, frame rails at the shock towers, rear quarters and floors — followed by whether the builder solved the known weak links (steering, brakes, cooling, wiring, fuel) or just bolted on lift and tires. A restomod with a crate engine and an overdrive-less or freshly rebuilt automatic is acceptable here; an undocumented 'built motor' with mystery fabrication is not.
profiles.weak_points: ["Rust is the defining issue and it is structural, not cosmetic. Check the rear quarter panels and inner wheel arches, the floor pans (especially under the driver's-side fuel tank on 1966–77 trucks that retain the under-seat tank), the tailgate skin and its lower corners, the rear crossmember, the windshield frame lower corners, and the cowl/kick panel area. Full quarter replacement with blend paint runs $3,000–$8,000 per side; a body-off metal restoration is $60,000–$150,000. Look for panel-gap irregularity, seam sealer that hides filler, and magnet/thickness-gauge evidence.", "Frame and body-mount corrosion. The front frame rails rot at the shock-tower/coil-spring mounts and at the radius-arm rear mounts; cracks propagate there from lift and oversize tires. Rotted body mounts let the tub shift and the doors stop closing. Weld-in frame stiffeners or repair plates are common and should be documented — new mounts and rail repair is $1,500–$5,000 of labor. Get clear underbody photos, not just 'no rust' claims.", '\'Bronco lean\' and worn front suspension. Sagging driver-side coil spring, tired radius-arm bushings, and a worn track bar / drag-link joint produce lean, wander, and shimmy-into-death-wobble at 45–60 mph, badly amplified by 33s and a 2.5" lift. Springs, bushings, shocks, and a full front end joint refresh is $1,200–$3,000; lifts done without correcting steering geometry or drop pitman arm create permanent bump steer.', 'Steering. Factory 1966–75 Ross cam-and-lever box (manual, or the weak Saginaw power box later) is vague and leaks; most good builds convert to a Saginaw power box or Borgeson unit with a new pitman arm and a hydraulic ram or quick-ratio setup. Verify the conversion is bolted through reinforced frame metal — cracked steering-box frame mounts are a known failure. Conversion cost $1,200–$2,500. Excessive on-center play or a leak at the box should be priced in.', 'Brakes. Front drums through 1975 (discs standard 1976–77) are marginal for modern traffic with big tires. Disc conversions (Wilwood/TOMS/Wild Horses, often with hydroboost) are common and desirable but must include a correct proportioning valve and sized master cylinder — symptoms of a bad job are long pedal travel, rear lockup, or no boost. Budget $1,500–$3,000 for a proper four-wheel disc/hydroboost job and inspect for fresh, correctly routed hard lines and a non-weeping booster.', "Fuel system. The original under-seat tank and sending units are a chronic problem: failing fuel gauges, cracked rubber fill hoses, weeping sender flanges, and fire risk from decades-old rubber lines under the cab. This listing's June 2026 sender and gauge replacement is exactly the typical item. A rear-tank relocation plus new lines and a properly rated in-tank pump for EFI is $800–$2,500; on EFI conversions, confirm return line, pump rating, and pressure regulator install quality.", 'Wiring and grounds. Original harnesses are brittle, the bulkhead connector and headlight/ignition switches overheat, and gauges read erratically. A complete American Autowire/Painless harness with a modern fuse box (as here) is a major plus; verify it was actually finished — look for loose splices, unfused add-ons, and LED-light or winch circuits tapped off the ignition. A proper rewire is $900–$1,500 in parts plus 20–40 hours labor.', 'Cooling. The stock radiator and shroudless fan are marginal; anything with a 302/347 stroker, big tires, and A/C or a body lift will run hot in stop-and-go or on a grade. Look for an aluminum crossflow radiator, correct shroud, and an electric fan setup with a proper relay. A 415 hp stroker in a 3,500-lb truck with 35s will also cook the transmission without an auxiliary cooler — confirm one exists.', "Drivetrain leaks and driveline angles. The Dana 20 transfer case seeps at the rear output seal and the shifter/housing gasket; twin-stick conversions can leak or pop out of gear if the detents and shift rails aren't right. Lifted trucks commonly vibrate f
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Replace tires — 2010 date codes are unsafe regardless of tread; a set of 33"–35" Toyo/BFG plus mount, balance, and alignment is $1,600–$2,400.', 'Full fluid service: engine oil, trans fluid and filter (fresh look at the rebuilt 4R70W), transfer case, both differentials, brake fluid flush, coolant.', 'Front-end inspection and retorque: radius arm bolts, track bar, drag link, tie rod ends, steering box mount, pitman arm nut; set toe and caster for the lift ($300–$800).', 'Brake system verification: bed-in, check hydroboost/master for weeping, confirm proportioning valve adjustment and parking brake function ($200–$600).', 'Chase leaks and finish-work items typical of a fresh build: fabricated engine mount inspection, exhaust hanger/clearance, fuel line routing and clamps, EFI fuel pressure
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Driveline vibration resolution if any remains: pinion angle shims, carrier bearing, or re-balance of the rear shaft ($400–$1,200).', 'Dana 20 rear output seal and shifter housing reseal; front axle knuckle/hub seal service ($600–$1,500).', 'EFI/ignition tuning and drivability sorting on the Sniper (idle, cold start, timing curve) plus possible distributor or coil work ($400–$1,000).', 'Seat, top, and weatherseal work: soft-top fit, windshield seam leak, door seals, and possible hardtop acquisition or refresh ($500–$3,000).', 'Cosmetic touch-in of documented chips/scratches on the tailgate and rear bumper corner; underbody cavity wax/rust-proofing given coastal Carmel air ($800–$2,000).', 'Gearing/final-drive reassessment if the truck feels under-geared on 35s, or a rear axle service if w
profiles.market_notes: Value is driven first by structure and documentation, then by build quality and taste: a rust-free, receipt-backed truck from a known builder (Icon, Gateway, Velocity, Kincer, TOMS/Wild Horses parts done well) sells far above a nice-looking backyard build. Uncut, original-spec 1966–68 examples — especially roadsters, Sports, and 1971–75 4-speed/V8 wagons with a Marti Report — command originality money, while tastefully executed restomods with fuel injection, four-wheel discs, power steering, and a modern overdrive automatic trade in a wide $45,000–$120,000 band. Color matters (factory-correct Brittany Blue, Wimbledon White, Boxwood Green read better than trendy repaints), as does a matching hardtop plus soft top; a color change away from the Marti-documented original costs some money with purists. Odometer readings are irrelevant; 'documented restoration with invoices in the gallery' is worth real dollars, and undocumented 415 hp claims are worth a discount.
profiles.catchup_notes: Even a freshly restored early Bronco needs a first-year sorting budget: 50-year-old rubber and hardware (tires, seals, hoses, body mounts, weatherstrip) and the inevitable punch-list of a recent build — leaks, fuel and wiring finish work, driveline angles, and brake/steering bedding. Assume everything not on a receipt is original and due, and add coastal rust-prevention (cavity wax, underbody treatment) immediately given Carmel's salt air.
