profiles.label: Porsche Cayman / Cayman S (987.2, DFI)
profiles.framing: The 987.2 is the sweet spot of the mid-engine Porsche line for a real-world driver: the 2009+ DFI engines (2.9 base, 3.4 S) shed the M96/M97 IMS bearing and bore-scoring anxiety that haunts the 987.1, and the chassis is still small, light, hydraulically steered, and immensely usable. For this buyer it is a Monterey Peninsula weekend and errand car that can also take Highway 1 or a canyon run without drama, and can absorb a real road trip with front and rear trunks. What matters most is documented maintenance from a Porsche specialist, an unmolested drivetrain and suspension, no track history, and a clean, complete car rather than the cheapest example. Options and transmission matter enormously to resale here — a well-optioned manual S in a real color is a different asset than a base-spec PDK.
profiles.weak_points: Water pump and thermostat: plastic impeller pumps are a consumable, typically 60k–90k miles or 8–10 years; symptoms are weeping from the pump vent hole, pink crust on the block, or slow warm-up. Budget $900–$1,600 installed; look for a receipt in the last ~60k. Coolant expansion tank and its cap crack with age — cheap parts, but a low-coolant light or crusty residue at the tank seam signals neglect. Radiators and A/C condensers sit low in the front bumper and pack with leaves and debris; corrosion-through causes coolant loss and the front radiator ducts trap moisture. Ask for photos of the front radiator area with the ducts removed and check for the debris-screen retrofit; a pair of radiators plus condensers is $1,800–$3,000. Rear main seal and AOS: the DFI engines are far better than 987.1 but still weep; a smoky cold-start plume or oil at the bellhousing means AOS ($700–$1,200) or RMS/clutch-out job ($2,000–$3,500 on a manual, more if the PDK must come out). Coil packs and DFI high-pressure fuel system: coil failure causes misfire codes and rough idle, cheap to fix; the high-pressure fuel pump and DFI injectors are the expensive tail — injector or HPFP work runs $1,200–$2,500. Carbon buildup on intake valves is inherent to direct injection; by 80k–100k expect mild hesitation and rough cold idle, walnut blasting $900–$1,500. PDK: the 7-speed dual-clutch is robust but requires fluid and filter service every ~40k miles at $700–$1,000; a neglected PDK with juddering low-speed engagement or delayed 1–2 shifts is a mechatronic/clutch-pack risk of $4,000–$9,000+. Demand a dated PDK service invoice, not a seller's recollection. Manual cars: dual-mass flywheel and clutch typically 60k–100k; a rattling clutch pedal at idle or high engagement point means $2,500–$3,500 with an RMS and IMS-free rear-end reseal. Suspension bushings and control arms: by 80k the rear toe links, front lower control arm bushings and top mounts are tired — squeaks over expansion joints, wandering alignment; a full round of arms and an alignment is $1,800–$3,500. Coilover conversions (Bilstein PSS9/PSS10) on an old car usually mean worn shock seals and a track past; PASM cars with a leaking OE damper are $1,000+ each. Rear decklid spoiler mechanism jams or throws a fault; motor/mechanism $600–$1,200. Ignition switch and the alarm/immobilizer module, plus the door-lock actuators and the microswitches in the doors, cause phantom drains and no-crank conditions; a parasitic draw complaint deserves investigation. Interior: soft-touch coating on the center console, glovebox and door pulls turns sticky with sun exposure; the Sport Chrono stopwatch bezel and the cupholder arms break. Bore scoring is largely a 987.1 issue but a borescope of all six cylinders and a leakdown are still the right money on any 15-year-old flat six. Finally, aftermarket high-flow cats: they routinely set P0420/P0430 and are not California-legal — a CEL from cats is a smog and registration problem in Carmel, not a cosmetic annoyance, and OE manifolds/cats to restore are $2,000–$4,000.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Fluids and filters if not documented within a year (engine oil, brake fluid on a 2-year cycle, coolant condition check). PDK fluid and filter service if there is no dated invoice within 40k miles. Full four-wheel alignment, especially on a coilover-equipped car. Tires: verify DOT dates — anything over 6 years old gets replaced regardless of tread, and mismatched front/rear brands (Michelin front, Continental rear as in the example) should be corrected to a matched staggered set, ~$1,400–$2,000. Brake pads and rotors if Hawk HP Plus track pads are fitted; those are unusable on the street (noise, cold bite) — swap to OE-spec pads and rotors, $1,200–$1,800. Diagnose and resolve any CEL: on a California-registered car, aftermarket cats setting P0420/P0430 must be addressed to pass smog, likely
profiles.repairs_12mo: Water pump and thermostat if not already replaced. Radiators and condensers if the front-end inspection shows corrosion or fin damage. Walnut-blast carbon cleaning and new spark plugs/coils at 90k–100k. Rear suspension bushings, toe links and drop links; front lower control arms if bushings are cracked. AOS if any cold-start smoke appears. Clutch and DMF on a manual approaching 90k. Serpentine belt, brake fluid flush, and a second oil service. Convertible-top items do not apply, but the rear spoiler mechanism and door-lock actuators are common one-off $600–$1,200 hits. Interior soft-touch trim refinishing if the sticky-coating problem is present.
profiles.market_notes: Manual transmission commands a meaningful premium over PDK on 987.2 Caymans and that gap has widened; PDK cars are the value play but sell slower. The S (3.4 DFI, 320 hp) is worth clearly more than the 2.9 base, and the Cayman R is a separate, much higher tier. Color and options drive the top of the market: PCCB-free but well-optioned cars in Guards Red, GT Silver, Aqua Blue, Peridot, or any PTS/special color with Sport Chrono, PASM, LSD, sport seats and full leather bring the money, while Arctic Silver over black is the most common and least differentiated combination. Documented Porsche-dealer or independent-specialist service history, a fresh PDK service, and a clean unmodified state are worth thousands; aftermarket cats, coilovers, harness bars and a CEL suggest track use and push a car firmly into the discount tier — realistically 15–25% under a stock, documented equivalent. Mileage bands matter less than records; 60k–90k with a binder beats 45k with a shrug.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 80k-mile 987.2 is now 15 years old and due for a full round of rubber and cooling: water pump/thermostat, coolant flush, expansion tank cap, radiator cleanout with debris screens, suspension bushings and toe links, and a fresh matched set of tires regardless of tread depth. DFI carbon cleaning and plugs land around 90k-100k. Plan roughly $4,000-$7,000 of catch-up in the first two years even on a well-kept car, and add the cost of restoring compliant catalytic converters if the car will be registered in California.

profiles.label: Saab 900 Turbo (Classic 900, 1979–1994)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the classic 900 Turbo is a charismatic, low-volume Swedish daily-driver — wraparound windshield, ignition on the console, a 16-valve B202 turbo with real mid-range shove, and a convertible body built by Valmet in Finland that is genuinely pleasant on Highway 1. It is not fast by modern standards and it is not a Porsche substitute; the appeal is the ergonomics, the torque curve, the airiness and the fact that almost none are left in honest, unmolested condition. The money question is never the purchase price, it is whether the car has been continuously maintained by someone who understood Saabs: oil-trap servicing, DI cassette, timing chain, and the transaxle-under-engine architecture that makes any clutch or chain job an engine-out event. Documented, stock, rust-free and cold-start-clean matters far more than mileage or a rare paint code.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Crankcase oil trap / PCV breather box (B202 turbo, effectively all mileages): the small mesh-and-baffle separator behind the intake clogs with sludge, pressurizes the crankcase and blows out the rear main, cam cover and dipstick seals, and in the worst case sludges the turbo feed. Cleaning is cheap ($100–300 with gaskets) if done every 30–50k; consequential damage is not. Look for receipts naming 'oil trap', 'breather box' or 'PCV service', and short (3–5k) synthetic oil intervals. 2) Turbocharger (Garrett T3, typically 100–160k): shaft play, oil seepage into the intake, smoke on spool-up, whistle changes. Rebuild/exchange $1,200–2,200 installed; wastegate actuator diaphragms also fail and cause overboost or lazy boost. 3) APC (Automatic Performance Control) boost/knock system: knock sensor, APC solenoid and the vacuum/boost hose web age out; symptoms are no boost, erratic gauge, or unrestrained overboost. Sensors/solenoids $150–400, hose sets cheap, diagnosis time-consuming. 4) Direct Ignition cassette (1988-on 16-valve): DI cassette and crank position sensor fail with age — misfire, no-start when hot, sudden stall. Genuine cassettes are $350–700 and getting scarce; a receipt within the last 10 years is a strong plus. 5) Timing chain, tensioner and guides (150k+ or any car with cold-start rattle): the single chain and plastic guides wear; a 2–5 second rattle at cold start is the tell. Job is $1,200–2,200 because of the tilted, transaxle-mounted engine layout. 6) Head gasket / cylinder head (120k+, worse on overheated or overboosted cars): coolant loss without external leak, white smoke, combustion pressure in the expansion tank. $1,800–3,000; add head skim/valve work. 7) Transaxle (the engine sits on top of the gearbox): 2nd-gear synchro crunch, differential/pinion whine, worn primary chain between crank and input shaft, and sloppy shift linkage bushings. Clutch replacement requires lifting the engine — $1,800–3,000 even when the clutch itself is a $400 part; assume the clutch is due if there is no receipt. 8) Oil leaks generally: rear main, sump gasket, cam cover, turbo oil return, and the power-steering rack/pump. Wet undersides are the norm; distinguish seep from streaming. 9) Convertible-specific: hydraulic top pump and rams leak (fluid in the trunk area, slow or one-sided operation), the top frame links and the header-rail/side seals harden and leak at the A-pillars, and the plastic rear window crazes. Frame/cylinder repair $800–2,500; a quality top installation is $2,000–4,000; original-pattern frame parts are scarce. Also check floor and footwell dampness from clogged cowl/plenum drains. 10) Rust: front subframe/crossmember and its mounting points, inner and outer sills and jacking points, floor pans, rear wheel arches, and — critically — the windshield surround under the wraparound glass, where a leaking screen rots the A-pillar base. Windshield-surround repair means glass out, $2,000–5,000+. 11) Cooling system: plastic-tank radiator, water pump, thermostat housing, hoses and heater control valve; heater core replacement is a dash-out job ($1,200–2,000). Any overheating history is a head-gasket flag. 12) Steering and front suspension: steering column lower U-joint and rack mounting bushings produce the classic 'play in the steering'; lower control arm bushings, upper strut mounts, sway-bar bushings and tie rods all wear in 60–80k cycles. A full front refresh is $1,200–2,500. 13) Electrical gremlins: bulb-failure sensor, ignition switch/steering lock in the console, power-window motors and regulators, headlight wiper motors, cornering-light and fog-light wiring, and dry/cracked engine-bay harness insulation. 14) Interior and trim: cracked dash top (often hidden by a molded dash cap — lift it and look), sagging headliner, broken seat-heater elements, brittle switch plastics, and pre-1993 A/C originally R12 — confirm whether it was properly converted to R134a (compressor, drier, hoses) or just topped off.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service including gearbox oil; remove and clean the crankcase oil trap/breather box and replace its gaskets; renew all vacuum/boost hoses and check APC function on a road test with the boost gauge; new plugs and (if undocumented) DI cassette; radiator/heater hose and belt inspection with replacement of anything 10+ years old; brake fluid flush plus inspection of rear calipers/flex lines; tighten up the steering column U-joint and rack bushings if the reported play persists after the 2026 work; clear the cowl and top-well drains, reseal or adjust the header rail and A-pillar seals, and service the convertible top hydraulics; alignment after any suspension work. Budget $1,500–3,000 at an independent Saab-literate shop.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Clutch and rear main seal if there is no receipt (engine-out, $2,000–3,000 combined and logically done together); front suspension bushings/struts/tie rods to remove the last of the vagueness; turbo inspection or exchange if shaft play or oil smoke appears; A/C compressor/drier and a proper R134a conversion if the system is weak; radiator and water pump on a 30+ year-old cooling system; exhaust from the downpipe back (original systems are long gone and aftermarket pieces fit poorly); convertible top frame links, side seals or a new top if the current one is aging; shift linkage bushings and a dash cap replaced with a proper repair if the underlying dash is cracked.
profiles.market_notes: Convertibles and SPG/Aero hatches carry a large premium over ordinary 900S cars; a 5-speed turbo is worth meaningfully more than an automatic, and automatics also suffer in the market for their fragility. Rare factory colors — Monte Carlo Yellow, Talladega Red, Edwardian Grey on an SPG — plus a documented window sticker, intact books and continuous service history can add 30–60% over a clean but anonymous example. Mileage matters less than evidence: a 130k car with oil-trap, DI, chain and top receipts routinely beats a 70k unknown, while Carfax accident entries, dash caps hiding cracks, non-original tops, aftermarket boost controllers or Hirsch/Abbott-style tuning without records all pull money out. Top of market for concours-level MCY convertibles has reached the mid-$20Ks–$30Ks; honest drivers sit $10,000–18,000.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 30-plus-year-old 900 needs a systematic rubber-and-seal catch-up: every vacuum/boost hose, coolant hose, fuel line, engine mount, suspension bushing and top seal is at or past end of life regardless of mileage. Plan $2,500–4,000 over the first two years just on age-related items, plus the engine-out clutch/rear-main job if no receipt exists, and source parts early through Saab specialists since classic 900 convertible and MCY-specific trim is drying up.

profiles.label: Subaru Forester 2.5 XT (SG, turbo)
profiles.framing: The SG Forester XT is the practical enthusiast answer to a WRX: same EJ255 turbo flat-four and AWD driveline in a tall, airy, cargo-friendly wagon with real ground clearance for Carmel-area fire roads and Sierra trips. For this buyer it is a do-everything daily that happens to run 13s, and the whole purchase decision hinges on one question: has this specific engine been detonated, over-boosted, or oil-starved by a previous owner. A documented, stock-tuned, well-maintained 5MT XT is a genuinely usable car; a mystery-tuned, big-turbo example is a short-block bill waiting to happen. Coastal California cars are a rust-exposure win, but salt-belt trade-ins circulate heavily in this model and must be inspected underneath before any price is agreed.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Ringland failure (EJ255, typically #4 piston) is the signature death of this engine — lean/knock events from aggressive or stale aftermarket tunes, cheap fuel, or a failing MAF/boost control. Symptoms: low compression on one cylinder, blow-by out the oil fill, puff of smoke at startup, rough idle. Cost: $5,000–8,000 for a quality short block install; expect leakdown/compression numbers as evidence before purchase. 2) Turbo (VF40) failure from oil-feed starvation: the banjo bolt at the turbo contains a fine filter screen that clogs with sludge and kills the bearing — Subaru issued the fix of replacing the bolt/screen and cleaning the oil pickup. Symptoms: whine, shaft play, blue smoke, boost drop. $1,500–2,500 installed; ask for receipts showing the banjo bolt/screen was addressed. 3) Head gasket weeping: turbo EJs use MLS gaskets so external coolant seepage is less common than in N/A 2.5s, but at 120k+ combustion-gas-into-coolant and oil seepage at the head-to-block joint do happen, often revealed by pressurized coolant, sweet smell, or a failed combustion-gas test — $2,200–3,200 with timing service bundled. 4) Timing belt, tensioner, idlers and water pump on a 105k-mile/8-year interval; a 2007 at 140k should show two services. Undocumented belt on an interference engine is a $1,200–1,600 immediate job or a catastrophic gamble. 5) Oil leaks: cam carrier/cam seals, valve cover gaskets (baked by turbo heat on the passenger side), front crank seal, and rear main seal — commonly $400–1,400 depending on how many are weeping and whether the timing cover is already coming off. 6) TGV (tumble generator valve) assemblies carbon up and stick, throwing P1152/P1153-type codes and rough running; delete plates or new assemblies $300–800. Related: PCV valve, clogged air/oil separator, and dirty MAF causing lean spikes. 7) Catalytic converter and knock-sensor codes: the factory pre-cat restricts and eventually crumbles (P0420), and the single knock sensor (P0325) is a cheap but critical part — cats $900–1,800, sensor $150–300. 8) Drivetrain: the 5MT (TY754) is the desirable spec but 2nd/3rd gear synchro wear, worn shifter bushings, and clutch life of 80–120k are normal; clutch with rear main seal $1,300–2,000. The 4EAT automatic with VTD is durable if fluid was changed but suffers torque-converter shudder and slow shifts, and a rebuild is $2,500–3,500. Mismatched-circumference tires destroy center differentials/transfer clutches — check all four tires for the same make, model and tread depth. 9) Rear wheel bearings (and front hubs) are a known wear item — growl that changes with load, $450–750 per corner. 10) Suspension age: front lower control arm bushings, rear trailing arm bushings, strut mounts, sway-bar end links and 20-year-old struts all together are a $1,200–2,500 refresh; sagging rear springs with cargo are typical. 11) Rust on non-California cars: rear wheel-arch lips, rocker seams behind the plastic cladding, rear subframe and lateral-link mounting points, strut tower tops, and the fuel-filler area. Perforation at subframe mounts is a structural walk-away. 12) Water intrusion: sunroof drain tubes clog and wet the headliner and A-pillars, rear hatch seals and the third brake light/hatch harness leak into the cargo area, and front quarter-window gussets leak onto the carpet — check for musty smell, stained headliner, and corroded rear-hatch wiring. 13) Electrical/interior wear: power window regulators, sunroof motor, failing dash cluster illumination, driver seat bolster and heated-seat elements, and a sagging headliner are all age-standard. 14) Modified examples: staged tunes, larger turbos, and E85 conversions are extremely common on this model and vastly increase risk — without a tuner's datalogs (knock/feedback correction, AFR), receipts for the fuel system, and an Accessport read of stored trouble codes, assume the engine is a lottery ticket.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service (oil with a quality filter, gearbox and front/rear diff fluid, coolant, brake fluid); replace all four tires with a matched set if there is any circumference mismatch; timing belt/water pump/tensioner/idler kit if not documented within 100k miles or 8 years; turbo oil-feed banjo bolt and oil pickup inspection/cleaning; new spark plugs and air filter; MAF cleaning; PCV valve; clear and re-read stored codes and knock data; address any active oil or coolant seep, sunroof drain cleanout, and worn sway-bar end links or strut mounts found on the test drive. Budget $1,800–3,500.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Clutch and rear main seal if the pedal is high or the car has 100k+ on the original; valve cover and cam carrier gaskets; one or two wheel bearings; struts/springs and control arm bushings; catalytic converter or O2 sensor for a P0420; radiator (plastic end tanks) and thermostat; front brake rotors/pads; battery, alternator or AC compressor as age items; possible TGV cleaning or delete and a return-to-stock or professionally re-verified tune. Budget $2,500–4,500.
profiles.market_notes: The 5MT XT Limited is the spec that moves money; automatics trade meaningfully cheaper and are harder to resell to enthusiasts. Documented timing-belt and head-gasket history, a stock or reputably tuned engine, and clean underbody (West Coast car) are worth more than low miles on a mystery car. WR Blue, Aspen White and the rarer 2008 Sports XT trim draw crowds, and heavily built JDM-STi-style cars occasionally clear $25k+ on auction sites — but that is enthusiast-auction money, not a floor for a driver-grade example, which is typically a $8k–16k car at 100–160k miles.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2007 XT is a 18-plus-year-old, 130k–160k-mile turbo car, so assume a deferred-maintenance catch-up round: timing belt kit and water pump, all fluids including diffs, plugs, PCV, coolant hoses and radiator, struts and bushings, one or two wheel bearings, and re-sealing the usual cam carrier and valve cover oil seeps. Plan $3,000–5,000 over the first year on top of purchase price even for a clean, documented example, and keep the short-block reserve intact until compression numbers prove the engine.

profiles.label: Toyota 4Runner N210 (4th Gen, 2003–2009)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the N210 is a 20-year-old body-on-frame family/adventure rig that should still be a low-drama daily driver: Highway 1 commuting, Big Sur trailheads, dump runs, and the occasional Sierra snow trip. The value proposition is Toyota durability plus real 4WD hardware, so the entire decision hinges on whether THIS truck has been kept out of salt and given honest fluid service — not on trim badges. A documented, unmodified, rust-free Western or Southern-dry example at 100–180k miles is a better buy than a low-mileage Rust Belt truck at any price. Automatic is the only transmission offered and is completely normal here.
profiles.weak_points: 1) FRAME AND UNDERBODY RUST is the single generation-defining risk. Midwest/Northeast trucks rot at the rear frame rails above the axle, the rear spring/shackle hangers, the crossmember behind the transfer case, and the body mounts. Toyota's frame rust campaigns largely covered Tacoma/Tundra/Sequoia, not the 4Runner, so there is no warranty backstop. Fresh black undercoating or 'fresh paint' on the underside of an auction truck from a salt state is a red flag, not a feature — it hides scale. A rotten frame is a walk-away, not a repair. 2) 'PINK MILKSHAKE' — on 2003–2005 (and some 2006) trucks the transmission cooler lives inside the radiator; when the internal barrier fails, coolant enters the ATF and destroys the A750F 5-speed. Symptoms: pink/strawberry-milkshake ATF on the dipstick, low coolant, harsh or slipping shifts. Prevention is a radiator replacement with an external cooler ($600–1,000); the cure after contamination is a transmission ($3,500–5,500 installed). Look for a radiator replacement receipt or verify clean red ATF and clean coolant. 3) REAR AIR SUSPENSION / X-REAS. Limited models (and some V8s) used a rear height-control air system whose bags, compressor and height sensors fail; Sport Edition used X-REAS cross-linked dampers with a center transfer valve. Both are expensive ($1,200–2,500 for OEM parts) and are commonly 'fixed' by converting to conventional coilovers/shocks — a conversion is acceptable but must be documented. Sagging rear, compressor running constantly, or a bouncy/uneven ride are tells. 4) LOWER BALL JOINTS. 2003–2007 front lower ball joints are a known wear/failure item, especially with lifts or aftermarket parts; a failure drops a corner. Check for grease boot tears, clunks over bumps, and insist on Toyota/OEM-quality parts in any receipt ($400–900/side installed). 5) DASHBOARD CRACKING/STICKINESS. Very common on N210 in sun-belt cars; Toyota's extended coverage has expired. Full dash replacement runs $1,200–2,500; a cap is $250–500. Cosmetic but it moves price. 6) 1GR-FE V6 OIL SEEPAGE at the cam towers, timing cover, and front main. A weep is typical by 150k; an actual reseal means pulling the timing cover, $2,000–4,000. Look for oil film on the front of the block and drips on the skid plate. Head gaskets are NOT a chronic 1GR failure — if coolant loss is present, suspect radiator/heater lines first, but a block test is cheap insurance on any truck with unexplained coolant use. 7) 2UZ-FE V8 TIMING BELT + water pump every 90k miles / ~9 years, $900–1,600. It's a non-interference engine so a break usually won't bend valves, but a dead water pump will cook it. No belt receipt on a V8 = assume you're buying one. 8) ABS/VSC BRAKE ACTUATOR. The ABS pump/actuator assembly fails with ABS+VSC+TRAC lights and sometimes a buzzing pump; new OEM assemblies run $1,500–2,500, rebuilt units $500–900. Verify all warning lamps extinguish after start. 9) POWER REAR WINDOW (tailgate glass). The regulator/motor and its wiring harness in the hatch fail, and a leaking tailgate seal rots the lower tailgate and the rear sill from the inside. Cycle the glass up and down from both the key and the dash switch; pull the cargo mat and look for standing water. 10) REAR HATCH/QUARTER AND WHEEL-ARCH ROT even on otherwise clean trucks — check behind the rear wheels, the rocker pinch welds, and under the rear bumper cover. 11) FRONT DIFFERENTIAL ACTUATOR (ADD) on part-time 4WD trucks leaks and sticks; full-time 4WD/locking-center-diff trucks use a Torsen center diff whose locker actuator can also fail. Any 4WD system must be range-shifted 2WD-4HI-4LO and, if equipped, center-diff-locked on a test drive. 12) EXHAUST/SECONDARY ITEMS OF AGE: cracked exhaust manifold studs on high-mile V6s, tired original struts (fronts commonly leak by 120k, $800–1,400 for a full set installed), steering rack and pump seeps, brittle radiator/heater hoses, and a heater blower resistor/AC amplifier that kills fan speeds. 13) HIGH-MILE V6 WATER PU
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service if records are thin: engine oil, ATF drain-and-fill (Toyota WS, no aggressive flush), front/rear diff and transfer case gear oil, coolant (Toyota SLLC), brake fluid. Replace the radiator with an external trans cooler on any 2003–2006 without a radiator receipt. Four tires if date codes are over 6 years old regardless of tread, plus an alignment. New wiper blades, cabin/engine air filters, and likely a battery. Expect a rear tailgate glass seal or regulator fix, a dash cap or trim tidy, and correcting any minor oil/coolant seep. Budget $1,500–3,000.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Struts/shocks all around if not recently done ($800–1,400), lower ball joints and possibly upper control arm bushings, front brake pads/rotors, serpentine belt and idler/tensioner, water pump and thermostat on a V6 over 130k, timing belt/water pump on any V8 without documentation ($900–1,600), front cam-tower or timing-cover seepage monitoring, wheel bearings/hub if there's a growl, and exhaust hardware. If it's a Limited or Sport with air suspension or X-REAS still fitted, budget for a documented conventional conversion ($1,000–1,800). $2,000–4,000 typical.
profiles.market_notes: Rust-free provenance is worth more than mileage on this generation — a 160k California/Arizona truck with clean frame photos regularly beats a 65k Illinois truck. V6 (1GR-FE) commands a premium over the V8 for most buyers because of the timing chain and better fuel economy, though V8 fans like the smoothness; the V8/Limited's rear air suspension is a price drag unless converted. Desirable spec: 4x4 with the locking center differential (full-time 4WD), rear locker on Trail/Sport trucks, cloth over cracked leather, sunroof, and no third-row (rare and space-eating anyway). Unmodified, one/two-owner cars with a real service file and 2009 facelift trucks sit at the top; lifted, big-tire, light-bar builds and any pink-fluid transmission history sit at the bottom.
profiles.catchup_notes: Treat any N210 as needing a full 20-year fluid and rubber reset: all gear oils, ATF drain-and-fill with Toyota WS, coolant, brake fluid, hoses, belt, and tires by date code rather than tread. Even a 64k-mile example will have hardened bushings, aged struts, dried tailgate/door seals, and an original radiator that is living on borrowed time. Budget roughly $2,000–3,500 in the first year for catch-up work on an otherwise sound, rust-free truck.

profiles.label: Toyota Land Cruiser 200-Series (URJ200, 5.7L 3UR-FE)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the 200-series is a lifetime-grade family/adventure truck: full-time 4WD, locking center diff, CRAWL control, 8,100 lb tow rating, and a 3UR-FE V8 that routinely sees 300k miles with fluids and attention. It is not a value play — it is a buy-once vehicle where the purchase price is often the smallest number in the first three years, so documented maintenance and a clean, unbypassed emissions system matter more than mileage. The 2008-2011 cars (pre-facelift, DVD nav, no Entune) are the cheap entry point but carry the generation's two most expensive known faults. In California, the smog transfer requirement makes emissions-system honesty a purchase gate, not a nice-to-have.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Secondary air injection system (2008-2011 especially): the AIS pumps, switching valves and air-injection driver fail from moisture ingestion, throwing P2440/P2442/P0418/P1441-family codes and a CEL that appears on cold starts. Toyota's ZE4 warranty enhancement (10yr/150k) has expired on a 2008. Dealer repair with both pumps and valves runs $3,000-4,500; independent with quality aftermarket parts $1,800-3,000. Bypass/delete kits and ECU tricks will fail a California smog inspection or leave incomplete readiness monitors — ask specifically whether the system is intact. 2) Cam tower / timing cover oil leaks on the 3UR-FE: Toyota reseals the cam towers under TSB; symptoms are oil weeping down the rear of the heads, oil in the valley, and drips onto the bellhousing/exhaust (burnt oil smell). Because the intake, timing cover and often the heads come off, expect $3,500-6,500. Very common at 120k-200k. 3) Starter motor lives under the intake manifold; when it fails (typically 150k-220k) it is a 6-10 hour job, $1,200-2,000. Smart owners do it preemptively with the water pump or air-pump work — look for that receipt. 4) Water pump and thermostat: whining/weeping around 100k-150k, $900-1,400 done properly with coolant and belt. 5) KDSS (Kinetic Dynamic Suspension System): hydraulic sway-bar system with cylinders and a valve body on the driver's frame rail. Look for oil film on the cylinders/lines and for the truck sitting cocked or with one front corner high; seized valves or a leaking accumulator is $1,200-2,500 and must be bled correctly. 6) Front suspension wear: upper control arm ball joints (integral, arm replaced, ~$500-800/side), lower ball joints, sway bar end links and bushings, and leaking front shocks/struts — the listed 'small leak from the front left shock' is textbook and means a pair at minimum ($600-1,400 for quality OE-spec or Bilstein/OME). 7) Brakes: the 200 is 5,800 lbs and eats pads and rotors; full four-corner pads and rotors $800-1,400. The ABS/VSC brake actuator (skid-control ECU/pump) is a known high-cost failure — a flashing VSC/ABS/brake light cluster can mean $2,000-3,500. 8) Drivetrain fluids: Toyota calls the AB60F six-speed 'lifetime' WS fluid; at 185k with no records assume a drain-and-fill service ($250-400) and budget for the possibility of a tired torque converter. Transfer case, front and rear diffs should be on a 30k cycle — no records means do all three now ($300-450). 9) Exhaust manifold/header cracks and broken manifold studs cause a cold-start tick and can mimic an air-injection code; repair $800-2,000. 10) Radiator end tanks and the intercooler-free cooling stack: plastic tank seepage and a clogged radiator around 150k+, $700-1,100. 11) Drive shaft: non-greaseable U-joints and center support bearings produce a driveline shudder at 40-60 mph; replacement shaft or rebuild $500-1,200. 12) Electronics of the 2008-2011 era: DVD-based navigation and Bluetooth are obsolete, rear-seat entertainment screens fail, the rear hatch struts sag, and the rear A/C evaporator can leak — none are fatal, but a head-unit swap is $500-1,500. 13) Frame and body rust: California cars are usually fine, but many 200s migrate from the Rockies/Midwest — inspect frame rails behind the rear wheels, the KDSS lines, brake lines and the rear crossmember. 14) Modification risk: lifted, re-geared, big-tire or 'delete' trucks are common in this platform; a lift without an OEM-correct KDSS-compatible setup causes driveline vibration and premature CV/ball joint wear.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Front shocks/struts in pairs and sway bar end links and bushings ($900-1,800 for the front end done properly); brake pads and likely rotors all around ($800-1,400); full fluid catch-up — engine oil, transmission drain-and-fill, transfer case, front and rear differentials, brake fluid flush, coolant if not documented ($700-1,100); new tires if the set is over 6 years old or mismatched ($1,200-1,700 in 285/60R18); serpentine belt, PCV valve, engine and cabin air filters, and iridium plugs if not done by 120k ($500-900 with plugs); alignment after suspension work ($150-250). If any CEL or incomplete readiness monitor exists, resolving it to pass California smog before or immediately after purchase.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Water pump/thermostat if not documented ($900-1,400); preemptive starter replacement done concurrently with any intake-off work ($1,200-2,000 standalone, far less as an add-on); secondary air injection pumps and valves if the system is original and untouched at this age ($1,800-3,500); upper control arms/ball joints ($1,000-1,600 the pair); cam tower reseal if any weep is developing ($3,500-6,500); radiator ($700-1,100); rear hatch struts, cabin blower resistor, and assorted 15-year-old rubber — bushings, hoses, hatch and door seals ($400-900); driveline center support bearing or U-joints if a shudder appears ($500-1,200).
profiles.market_notes: There is one US trim, so price moves on mileage bands, records, rust history, and whether the air-injection and cam-tower jobs are already done with receipts — a documented sub-150k California truck with those two items addressed commands a real premium over an undocumented 185k example. 2008-2011 cars are the value tier; the 2013+ facelift and especially 2016+ (8-speed, Safety Sense, Entune) step up several thousand dollars. Neutral colors with tan or grey leather and unmolested stock suspension sell fastest to this buyer type; big lifts, aftermarket bumpers and light bars narrow the buyer pool and add hidden wear. At 185k a clean, documented example in Northern California realistically trades in the low-to-mid $20s, so anything near $26k needs receipts, not just a seller's summary of a PPI.
profiles.catchup_notes: A 15-year-old, 185k-mile 200-series should be assumed to need a full fluid reset (transmission, transfer case, both diffs, coolant, brake fluid), a front-end refresh of shocks, links and bushings, and new tires — roughly $3,000-4,500 before touching the two headline jobs. The secondary air injection system and the cam tower reseal are the budget-defining unknowns: if neither has receipts, plan for one or both within two years. Everything else on this truck is ordinary Toyota wear that rewards preemptive work, especially bundling the starter with any intake-off service.

profiles.label: Toyota Land Cruiser 80-Series (FZJ80 / FJ80)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the 80-Series is a slow, heavy, deeply over-engineered family 4x4 that can do Carmel-to-Big-Sur duty on Monday and Alabama Hills or the Sierra on Friday, and still be fixable in a home garage twenty years from now. The car to want is a documented, mostly-stock 1993-1997 FZJ80 with the 1FZ-FE, factory front and rear lockers if possible, a legible service history on the head gasket, birfields, radiator and cooling system, and California/dry-state provenance so the frame and rear body seams are solid. Because these are all 28-35 years old with 150k-300k miles, value lives almost entirely in documentation and rust, not mileage. Modification level matters: a tasteful mild lift and bumpers are acceptable, but engine/trans swaps of unknown provenance, mileage inconsistencies, and undocumented drivetrain work should be priced as risk, not as features.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Head gasket on the 1FZ-FE: the factory gasket typically lets go somewhere between 150k and 250k miles, often as coolant loss with no external leak, combustion gases in the coolant, or overheating on grades. A proper job includes head resurfacing, ARP or new OEM head bolts (the factory bolts are torque-to-yield and stretch), new intake/exhaust gaskets and a cooling-system refresh; expect $2,500-$4,500 at a shop. Look for a dated invoice naming the head gasket, head machining, and bolt type. 2) Birfield joints and front axle service: knuckle seals weep, the moly grease and gear oil mix, and clicking/popping on full-lock turns signals worn birfs. A full front axle 'birf job' with new birfields, knuckle seals, wheel bearings, and trunnion bearings runs $1,200-$2,500; a leaking knuckle that's been ignored also wrecks wheel bearings and can contaminate the front brakes. 3) Rust: the classic spots are the rear quarters above the wheel arches, the rear hatch/tailgate lower seam, the area beneath the rear window (a known water trap on these, exactly as noted in the example listing), floor pans under the rear cargo mat, the rear crossmember and frame rails behind the rear wheels, and the third-member/skid area. Frame rust near the rear spring hangers is a structural dealbreaker. 4) Cooling system: original brass radiators crack at the plastic tanks, the fan clutch goes soft, hoses and the heater T's fail; a full refresh (radiator, clutch, hoses, thermostat, cap, flush) is $800-$1,500 and is cheap insurance against another head gasket. 5) Power steering and brake system: PS pump and gearbox seep, and the hydro-boost/brake booster accumulator ('boost accumulator') on ABS-equipped trucks fails, giving a hard pedal and an intermittent brake warning light; accumulator is roughly $400-$900 installed and the ABS pump assembly is much worse. 6) Rear main seal, oil pan gasket, and front crank seal weeps are common at 200k+; not urgent but budget $600-$1,500 if combined with other work. 7) A440F/A442F four-speed automatic: generally robust but dark, burnt fluid or a shudder in lockup means a rebuild ($2,500-$4,000). Ask for drain-and-fill records; these were often never serviced. 8) Front and rear axle/differential seals and the factory e-locker actuators: locker motors and the wiring/vacuum for the CDL and lockers fail, and the dash locker lights blink without engaging. Confirm both lockers actually engage on a lift, not just that the buttons light up. 9) Suspension bushings, radius arm bushings, panhard and sway bar bushings, and steering damper are all worn out at this age; a full bushing and shock refresh is $1,200-$2,500 and transforms the driving feel. Lifted trucks with poor geometry wander and eat tires. 10) Electrical gremlins: door lock actuators, power window regulators, sagging headliners, cracked dash tops, failing ABS sensors, dead gauge cluster lights, and the notorious A/C evaporator/expansion valve and rear A/C lines on dual-A/C trucks; an R-12-to-R134a conversion done badly cools poorly. 11) Odometer and identity risk: many 80s have had clusters swapped, engines swapped, or Carfax mileage inconsistencies. Without a provenance trail the true mileage on the chassis and drivetrain is unknowable, which is what happened on the example truck. 12) Exhaust manifold and downpipe studs on the 1FZ shear and hiss; heat shields rattle. Minor but annoying, $300-$800. 13) Fuel pump, injector seals, and 30-year-old vacuum/PCV lines cause rough idle and hot-start issues; a full rubber-line refresh is a weekend and $150 in parts. 14) Tire and gearing mismatch: 33-35" tires on stock 4.11 gearing with the automatic makes an already-slow truck painful and raises EGTs and trans temps; re-gearing is $2,000-$3,500 per axle pair.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service (engine oil, both diffs, transfer case, trans drain-and-fill, brake fluid, coolant); cooling-system assessment and likely radiator, fan clutch, hoses, thermostat and cap; block test / combustion-gas test on the coolant and act on the result; front axle knuckle inspection with new knuckle seals and repack of birfields if any weep or clicking; new tires if age-cracked or mismatched; brake pads, rotor check, and boost accumulator if the pedal is hard; battery, belts, wiper blades; replace all accessible 30-year-old vacuum and coolant hose sections; alignment after any suspension work. Budget $1,500-$3,500 on a good example.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Head gasket if not documented as done with resurfaced head and upgraded bolts; complete suspension bushing and shock refresh including radius arm bushings, panhard, sway bar links and steering damper; power steering pump/gearbox reseal; rear main or oil pan seal if dripping; A/C system service or evaporator/expansion valve work; locker actuator repair or rewire; door lock actuators, window regulators, headliner; rust remediation on rear quarters, hatch seam and under-rear-window area before it spreads; possible re-gear if running oversize tires. Realistic 12-month spend $3,000-$7,000 depending on head gasket status.
profiles.market_notes: Price is driven by rust-free body, documented head gasket and birfield service, and factory front/rear lockers (1993+ and especially 1995-1997 Collector's Edition style trucks with both lockers command a real premium). Low-mileage (sub-150k) unmolested examples with original paint, clean two-owner histories and no lift trade at strong multiples of high-mileage lifted trucks; mileage inconsistency, engine or transmission swaps of unknown origin, and heavy overland builds all compress value regardless of parts spend. Desirable colors are the factory whites, greens and the deep blues/greys with tan or grey leather; aftermarket bumper/winch/drawer builds rarely return their cost. Dry Southwest and California cars are worth a meaningful premium over Midwest/Northeast trucks, and a well-sorted driver-quality FZJ80 typically lands in the high teens to low thirties with exceptional low-mile lockered examples pushing past $45k.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 30-year-old truck needs a full deferred-maintenance reset regardless of how well it drives: cooling system, all fluids, front axle knuckle service, suspension bushings and shocks, brake hydraulics, and every rubber hose and seal. Even a strong example should be bought with $5,000-$8,000 set aside so the head gasket or birfields can be done on your schedule rather than on the side of Highway 1.

profiles.label: Volvo Amazon 122S Wagon (P220)
profiles.framing: This is a charming, genuinely usable 1960s wagon that the buyer will drive on Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road, not a trailer queen. Mechanically it is simple, over-built, and fully supported by the aftermarket (VP Autoparts, Skandix, IPD), so the real questions are rust, brakes, front-end wear, and whether the car has been honestly sorted or merely made pretty. On a 4-speed non-overdrive car with a 4.10-ish final drive, 65-70 mph is a buzzy 3,400-3,700 rpm — acceptable for local use, tiring for long freeway hauls, and the single biggest driveability limit worth pricing in. Documentation matters more than shine: a repainted car with a bypassed heater, dead horn, and dead parking brake is telling you where the money went.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Structural rust is the only true value-killer. Check the front frame rails/torque boxes ahead of the firewall, the jacking points and rocker/sill closing panels, the floor pans under both front seats, the battery tray area, and — wagon-specific — the rear cargo floor, the spare-tire well, the rear spring hangers/shackle mounts, and the D-pillar/rear arch seams. A repaint in 2021 with 'spots of overspray' means the underside and seams must be photographed, not assumed. Cut-and-weld floor/rocker repair runs $1,500-$5,000+; frame-rail or spring-hanger repair can exceed the car's value. 2) Wagon tailgate rust: the lower gate's inner skin and bottom seam and the upper gate's glass frame trap water; hinges sag and the upper latch wears (rebuilt latches are available ~$150-300). A rusted lower gate is a hard-to-source, expensive panel. 3) King-pin front suspension (not ball joints): pins and bushings need grease every ~1,500 miles and are almost always neglected. Symptoms: clunk over bumps, wander, uneven front tire wear, vertical play when levered at the wheel. Proper rebuild with reaming/line-boring of the new bushings is $800-1,800 for the pair; shops that just press bushings in produce a car that binds. 4) Steering box (Bishop cam / cam-and-roller) develops 2-4 inches of play at the rim; also idler arm, tie rod ends, and the drag link. Rebuild box $500-900 exchanged, plus $300-600 in links. 5) Brakes: front Girling discs with rear drums; 1967 cars use a dual-circuit master. Expect seized caliper pistons, weeping wheel cylinders, and 30-year-old flex hoses. The parking brake acting on the rear drums seizes at the cables and levers constantly — 'parking brake doesn't work' is normal, and it is both a safety and a California-registration/inspection annoyance. Full system refresh (master, calipers, wheel cylinders, hoses, shoes, pads, cables) is $1,200-2,200. 6) B18B engine (dual SU HS6 carbs, ~95 hp): the five-main bottom end is famously durable, but the camshaft drive gear is a fiber/composite gear that strips teeth without warning, typically past 80-100k miles or after decades of age — a $60 part that requires the timing cover off ($400-800 labor); an aluminum-hub steel/fiber replacement receipt is exactly what you want to see. 7) Oil leaks: rear main and front crank seal weep, and a clogged 'flame trap' (PCV oil trap) in the intake pressurizes the crankcase and pushes oil past every seal. Cleaning/replacing the flame trap and hose is a $40 fix that prevents a $1,200 diagnosis. 8) Twin SU carbs go out of sync as throttle shafts and jet seals wear: hard cold starts, uneven idle, plug fouling, 16-18 mpg where 24-26 is normal. Rebuild/rebush the pair $500-900; many cars have been 'fixed' with a single Weber downdraft conversion, which runs but is a de-originalizing move. 9) Cooling: original radiators are usually clogged or already recored; water pump, thermostat housing corrosion, and hardened hoses are routine. Recore $400-650. Watch for overheating in traffic — a sorted Amazon should not. 10) Heater system: the box, valve, and core are buried behind the dash and the valve seizes; 'heater bypassed' is a common shortcut. Restoring heat/defrost properly means core rebuild plus box removal, $800-1,800. No defroster is a real problem in Carmel fog. 11) Electrical: many 1967 cars still have a generator/regulator (alternator conversion $350-700), plus corroded fuse block and ground straps, failed horn ring contact, dead wiper motors, and brittle cloth-loom wiring at the headlight switch and column. A dead radio/horn usually signals an un-restored harness. 12) Drivetrain: M40 4-speed is stout but the clutch hydraulics (master/slave) and the clutch cross-shaft bushings wear; second-gear synchro is the first to go. The Spicer rear axle leaks at the pinion seal and the axle-tube/backing-plate seals contaminate rear shoes. Retrofitting an M41 with Laycock J-type overdrive is the single best driveability upgrade, $2,000-3,500 installed — an
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full brake safety pass: flex hoses, wheel cylinders, caliper rebuild/replacement, fluid flush, and parking brake cables/levers freed and adjusted ($900-1,800). Replace all rubber fuel lines and inspect the tank/pump ($250-500). Flame trap/PCV service and full fluid change including gearbox and rear axle ($200-350). Twin SU sync, points/condenser/cap/rotor, valve adjustment, timing ($400-800). Front-end inspection with king-pin grease service and tie-rod/idler tightening; expect a king-pin rebuild if there is measurable play ($800-1,800). Re-commission the horn and wipers (safety/registration) and diagnose the bypassed heater ($300-900). Fresh date-coded tires if the current set is over six years old ($700-1,000). Seat-belt condition and mounting check.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Camshaft fiber-gear replacement if there is no receipt ($500-900 installed). Radiator recore and cooling-system refresh including water pump and hoses ($700-1,200). Heater core/valve restoration for real defrost ($800-1,800). Alternator conversion and fuse-block/ground-strap refresh ($500-1,000). Steering box rebuild or exchange plus idler arm ($700-1,400). Rear main/front seal and pinion-seal attention if oil consumption or drips persist ($600-1,500). Weatherstrip and tailgate seal replacement to stop cargo-floor water intrusion ($800-1,800). Seat cushion and headliner repair ($800-2,000). Strongly consider an M41 overdrive gearbox swap for freeway usability ($2,000-3,500). Localized rust repair on rockers/jack points/spare well if the PPI finds early scale ($1,500-4,000).
profiles.market_notes: Wagons (P220) command a clear premium over 122S sedans and two-doors; a 4-speed is essential, an original overdrive (M41) car adds roughly $2,000-4,000, and the rare BW35 automatic subtracts heavily. Documented rust-free dry-state provenance, photographed underside, and a receipt file move price more than paint gloss — driver-quality repainted cars with deferred mechanicals cluster around $9,000-16,000, genuinely sorted examples with overdrive, working heat, and a brake/front-end file reach $20,000-30,000, and true restorations go higher. Period colors with the split tailgate, correct 15-inch steels with hubcaps, and honest unmolested engine bays (twin SUs, not a Weber) support the top of the band; East Coast/Southeast cars carry a rust discount plus $1,200-1,800 shipping to the Monterey Peninsula. Non-functioning heater, parking brake, and horn are cheap-sounding items that reliably knock $1,500-3,000 off bidder confidence because they signal an unfinished car.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a ~58-year-old car needs a full safety re-commission regardless of cosmetics: all brake hydraulics and flex hoses, all rubber fuel lines, cooling system, weatherstrip, and date-expired tires. Budget $3,500-6,000 in the first year just to bring deferred rubber, brakes, and front-end wear current, plus $2,000-3,500 more if you want overdrive and working heat/defrost for real Monterey Peninsula use.

documentation.rationale: Strong on identity and terms: full VIN published and matching the decode, stock reference, itemised equipment, a clearly stated all-fees-included price, a named dealer with address and phone, and an Autotrader history panel reporting single owner and no reported accident or damage. Empty on maintenance and condition evidence: an unusually long list of major work (timing belt, water pump, radiator, CV axles, control-arm bushing, all four brakes) is asserted in capital letters with no invoice, no date, no mileage and no photograph of any of it, and the history report itself is not attached. On a 2004 V8 where the timing-belt record is the primary price driver, claimed-only is worth little.

condition.rationale: The one attached photo of this actual car shows a straight, clean Nautical Blue body, correct-looking headlights, matched bronze Method wheels and new-looking all-terrains, no visible damage or mismatched panels. A one-owner Southern California GX at 117k is a favourable baseline and the claimed refresh, if real, covers the model's top failure points. But there is no interior, engine-bay, undercarriage, frame or dash photo of this VIN in the attached set, no scan data, and the rear air-suspension delete quality is entirely unassessed — several of the model's worst-case items are simply unexamined here.

price_value.rationale: $25,995 before tax and registration is at the very top of the GX470 market and this profile explicitly notes that heavily modified builds trade at a discount to clean stock examples with records. Comparable sold cars: a 2008 with 129k at $24,000 on BaT, a 2004 with 161k at $15,500, a 2006 with 154k at $16,500 in Downey, a 2003 with 168k at $11,300 in Fremont. Active West Coast peers include a 90k-mile 2006 Sport bidding at $15,888 in Belmont. The 117k mileage and one-owner blue spec are genuinely better than most, and new tires plus an OME kit are real money, but the buyer is being charged full retail for a dealer build whose service claims are unpapered — that is paying a premium for unverified work.

mission_fit.rationale: Body-on-frame V8, real 4WD, roof rack and a big square cargo area do serve dogs, gear, a sleeping platform or a rooftop tent, and an automatic is fine for this branch. But the profile's own catch-up note warns that a GX overlaps the household RX 350 and should only be recommended when the body-on-frame off-road capability is itself wanted — and Jason states pure off-roading is not planned. The 2-inch lift and 285/70R17 all-terrains add nothing he needs while costing mpg, ride quality and tire dollars, and the profile treats an existing build as modest value at most.

logistics.rationale: San Diego is about 372 miles from Carmel — a straightforward same-day drive home or a fly-and-drive, and the return trip doubles as a long shakedown. It is a fixed-address dealer open Tuesday–Saturday, so a San Diego independent Toyota/Lexus specialist PPI should be arrangeable, though the ad never addresses inspection access. Already a California car, so registration and smog are routine; the advertised price includes dealer fees with tax and DMV on top.

emotional_spec_fit.rationale: Nautical Blue over tan with bronze wheels is a genuinely attractive, tastefully executed combination and non-navigation is the preferred spec for a car of this age. It is a solid, characterful truck — but it is not the enthusiast brief at all (no manual, no sporting character) and it duplicates a utility role the RX already covers, so it carries little of the emotional pull of the MINI/GTI/128i/Z3 shortlist.

positives: One-owner, no-reported-accident Southern California GX470 at a relatively low 117,000 miles for the model — the dry-state, single-owner profile is exactly the right starting point and avoids the frame-rust hard reject.

Lower ball joints (recall-history item), steering rack, tie rods and the newly claimed CV axles and boots.
Driveline check with the 2-inch lift: driveshaft angles, center support bearing, vibration at 60–75 mph on the test drive.
Transfer case and differential fluid condition — pull plugs and look at what comes out.
Dashboard surface condition to confirm the recall replacement, plus sunroof drains and operation.
what_would_change_verdict: Dated, mileage-stamped invoices for the timing belt, water pump and radiator plus the actual history-report PDF would move documentation and condition up substantially and make this a genuinely sorted example.
A clean independent Toyota/Lexus PPI on a lift — no frame corrosion, no stored codes after the AHC delete, correct ride height and driveline angles — would answer most of the open questions at once.
A negotiated price in the low-$20,000s, reflecting that modified builds trade under clean stock examples with records, would repair the weakest rating.
Refusal to release the car for an off-site PPI, or an inability to produce a single invoice for the advertised service list, should end this immediately.
Discovery of active AHC/VSC lamps, a cheap or unaligned lift, or frame corrosion would push this to a reject regardless of price.
evidence.mission_note: This is the capability branch and the automatic is fine, but the GX470 duplicates the RX 350's role and Jason has said pure off-roading is not planned, so the lift and 33-inch all-terrains buy capability he does not want while costing ride, fuel and tires. It only earns a place if body-on-frame V8 toughness and a rooftop-tent-capable platform are wanted for their own sake — and at this asking price it is not the efficient way to buy that.
evidence.rationale: This is an attractive one-owner Southern California GX470 with genuinely good bones — 117k miles, Nautical Blue over tan, non-navigation, no reported accident, and a claimed refresh that targets precisely the model's failure points — but essentially none of the mechanical story is documented. The two items that set GX470 value, the timing-belt record and the rear-suspension status, are both unpapered here: the belt is claimed in the ad with no date or mileage, and the air ride has been eliminated in favour of an Old Man Emu 2-inch lift whose kit quality, alignment and residual fault codes are undescribed. The single attached photo of this car shows a straight, clean truck on four matching Method wheels with visibly new all-terrains, which supports the tire claim; the remaining attached images are other cars on the dealer's lot, so the interior, engine bay, dash and undercarriage of this VIN are not examined here. Price is the hardest number to defend: $25,995 plus tax and DMV sits above a 129k-mile 2008 that sold for $24,000 on BaT and well above the $11,300–$16,500 band where most comparable West Coast GX470s have traded, and this profile states that modified overland builds trade at a discount to stock examples with records, not a premium. Logistics are good — a fixed San Diego dealer 372 miles from Carmel, drivable home, already California-registered — and PPI access should be arrangeable, though the ad is silent on it. Against the mission, the truck duplicates the RX 350 and adds off-road hardware Jason has said he does not need. The route forward is simple and falsifiable: invoices and a lift inspection, then a price conversation; without the paper this is full retail for claims.
evidence.next_action: Call Miramar Motorsports and ask them to email the dated, mileage-stamped invoices for the timing belt/water pump and radiator plus the full Carfax PDF, and to confirm in writing that the car can go to an independent San Diego Toyota/Lexus specialist for a lift PPI before any deposit.

what_would_change_verdict: A dated Lexus or independent specialist report clearing the 08/07/2026 temperature-gauge and light-flicker complaint, plus a clean cooling-system pressure test and a scan with no stored or permanent codes, would move this up materially.

A body shop invoice and pre-repair photos showing the July 2026 damage was a cosmetic front bumper strike only, with no radiator-support or structural involvement, would neutralise the biggest documentation conflict.

A lift inspection confirming no frame corrosion after the Alaska years, correct rear shock installation with no noise, and a matched set of tires with recent date codes would support the asking price.
Evidence of a recurring or unexplained temperature/electrical fault, frame corrosion, or a P2440/P2442 code would drop this below consideration at this money.
A negotiated price meaningfully below the $25,040 ask — reflecting the damage report, the twice-done rear brakes and the outstanding 13-year fluid catch-up — would improve the risk-adjusted value.
evidence.mission_note: As the utility_capability branch this does deliver what the RX 350 cannot — body-on-frame, low range, tow package, third row and factory roof rails for a rooftop tent or sleeping platform — so it is not merely a second RX. But it is a capability purchase that consumes most of the price ceiling while leaving the enthusiast-bridge need created by the 335i entirely unsolved, so it should be judged strictly as a pragmatic capability buy and only bought if the open temperature-gauge and damage questions close cleanly.
evidence.rationale: This is the best-documented private listing in the set and simultaneously the one with the most unresolved recent history. The Carfax and Lexus repair-order printout verify 63,363 miles with no rollback indication, a guaranteed clean California title, three owners, all recalls performed, and a genuine recent spend at Lexus dealers: both front struts (Jan 2026, found blown at 61k), both rear shocks (Jul 2026), front brakes (Aug 2025) and rear brakes twice (Feb and Jul 2026). Against that, the documents contradict the listing's 'No Accident or Damage Reported' banner — Carfax shows minor damage on 07/24/2026 and the 07/16/2026 order shows a sublet front bumper replacement the seller advertises as a feature. More seriously, the Lexus Escondido order of 08/07/2026 records the owner reporting a temperature gauge swinging hot and cold with dash lights flickering on inclines, and declining any diagnostic; on a 1UR-FE whose known weak points are valley-plate coolant leaks and secondary air injection, with no coolant service documented in thirteen years, that symptom is exactly the thing that cannot be left unexamined. The August 2025 pothole, the twice-repeated rear brake job, the owner's own cluster-tampering question that Lexus could not resolve, and a Bureau of Automotive Repair case all form a cluster of activity in the month before the car was listed. Price at $25,040 tracks the $24,420 Carfax value and is fair for a low-mile California car, but it is a base/Convenience trim, it sits close to the $27,000 maximum, and the fluid catch-up plus the diagnostic work are still ahead. Logistics are the strongest part of the picture: Palm Desert is an easy trip, the car is well known to four Lexus dealers, and the seller proposes closing at a dealership, so a genuine PPI is realistic. Contingent interest, not a buy at the ask until the temperature-gauge complaint and the damage event are documented closed.
evidence.next_action: Message the seller for the body-shop invoice and pre-repair photos behind the 07/24/2026 damage report, and book a pre-purchase inspection at an independent Toyota/Lexus specialist near Palm Desert with an explicit brief to pressure-test the cooling system, scan for permanent/history codes including P2440/P2442, and lift-inspect the frame — before discussing price.

Water pump replacement is claimed but nothing is said about the OEM plastic-tank radiator (a known failure that can send coolant into the transmission), front cover/cam seal weeping, power-steering leaks or brake condition beyond a claimed brake job.

documentation.rationale: Identity and terms are solid: VIN, stock number, full equipment list, a single itemised cash price with dealer fees included, a named dealer with address and phone, and an AutoTrader VHR badge. Maintenance and condition evidence is empty: a 221,000-mile truck whose entire service story is one all-caps sentence, with no invoices for the timing belt, water pump, CV axles or brakes, no full history report, no scan and no undercarriage or interior photos. Category (a) earned, category (b) unearned.

condition.rationale: The silver car photographs straight and clean, sits evenly on a modest OME lift with four matching all-terrains, and the claimed work list (timing belt/water pump, CV axles, brakes front and rear, air-ride delete) is exactly the right list for this platform if it was actually done. Against that: 221,000 miles, no engine bay, undercarriage, dash or cluster images, nothing on the plastic-tank radiator, exhaust manifolds, transmission/transfer case/diff service, lower ball joints or the 2008 secondary-air system. Unknowns dominate the areas that cost the most.

price_value.rationale: $16,995 (dealer fees included) sits at the level recent auction results assigned to 90k–160k-mile GX470s — the 2006 at 154,500 mi sold $16,500, a 2006 Sport at 90k is bidding $15,888 — while 200k-plus examples sold at $8,400–$11,600. The build and the claimed service list explain part of the premium, and the market note that modified overlands trade at a discount to documented stock cars cuts the other way. Undocumented, it is a full retail price for a very high-mileage truck; with receipts and a clean PPI it becomes defensible, particularly if negotiated down.

mission_fit.rationale: This is genuine body-on-frame V8 4WD with low range, a roof rack, a flat load area for dogs and gear and enough payload for a sleeping platform or roof tent — capability the RX 350 does not supply. But it also duplicates the RX as a three-row-ish family hauler, and as a bridge to replace the 335i it brings 221k miles and an air-ride-deleted dealer build rather than a documented survivor. It only justifies itself if the off-pavement capability itself is wanted.

logistics.rationale: San Diego, roughly 372 miles from Carmel — an easy fly-or-drive and an easy drive home. It is a physical dealer lot open Tuesday–Saturday, so an independent PPI in San Diego is straightforward to arrange in principle; California dealer sale normally carries a smog certificate. Deductions because PPI permission and record access are untested and the ad answers no technical questions.

emotional_spec_fit.rationale: Silver over gray with a tasteful 2-inch lift and all-terrains is a handsome, sensible look, and the GX470 has real character as a Land Cruiser Prado underneath. It is not the enthusiast brief at all — automatic, no manual, no sports-car reward — and per the buyer's own rule the accessories add modest value only, never substituting for evidence.

positives: Right platform for the capability mission: 2UZ-FE V8, full-time 4WD with low range, roof rack, dog/gear-friendly cargo area — none of which the RX 350 provides.

The claimed work list targets exactly the GX470's known weak points: timing belt and water pump, serpentine belt, CV axles, brakes front and rear, and elimination of the failure-prone rear air suspension with an OME setup.
Southern California car at a physical dealer 372 miles away — trivial to arrange a PPI and to drive home; VIN, stock number and an itemised all-in dealer price are published.

Toyota/Lexus mechanicals mean 221,000 miles is a yellow flag rather than a disqualifier, and Jason's mechanic recommends the brand.
concerns: Observed: every major service on this car is a seller sentence in the advertisement — no dated, mileage-stamped invoice for the timing belt, water pump, CV axles or brakes. On a 221,000-mile belt engine that is the difference between a bargain and a $3,000 surprise.

Observed: $16,995 is the price recent sales assigned to 90k–160k-mile GX470s, while 200k-plus examples cleared $8,400–$11,600; the premium rests entirely on undocumented claims and a dealer build the market typically discounts.

Observed: the factory rear air suspension has been eliminated and a 2-inch lift installed by the seller, with no kit part numbers, install invoice, alignment sheet or confirmation that the AVS/height-control system was properly retired rather than the dash light simply suppressed.

Unverified: no dash-lights photo or OBD-II scan, and a 2008 GX470 carries secondary air injection — a classic permanent-MIL and smog-readiness problem (ask for a key-on dash photo and a full scan including readiness monitors).

Unverified: the OEM plastic-tank radiator and transmission cooler, transmission, transfer case and differential fluid history at 221k, exhaust manifold cracks and lower ball joints are all unaddressed by the listing (inspect and ask for receipts).

ppi_focus: Verify the timing belt job physically: belt condition/markings, water pump weep hole, cam and crank seal dryness, idler and tensioner condition.
Frame rails, rear crossmember, body mounts and underbody for corrosion and for any evidence of hard off-road contact under the modest lift.
OEM plastic-tank radiator: pressure test, check for pink crust, and inspect transmission fluid colour/smell for coolant intrusion.
Secondary air injection system function and full readiness-monitor status before committing to a California registration.
Rear air-ride delete quality: spring and shock brand, correct rear height, bump-stop and brake-line/ABS-line clearance, AVS wiring disposition and any suppressed fault.
Lower ball joints (recall history), upper control arms, steering rack and idler arm, plus a post-lift alignment check and driveline vibration at highway speed.
Exhaust manifolds for the classic cold-start tick/cracking, and catalytic converter condition.
Transmission fluid condition and pan inspection, transfer case and front/rear differential fluid, and front differential actuator (ADD) engagement in 4-Lo.
CV axle install quality: boot condition, hub nut torque, ABS tone-ring signals, any clicking on full lock.
Cabin: dash cracking, sunroof operation and drains, rear HVAC, and all power accessories.
what_would_change_verdict: Dated, mileage-stamped invoices for the timing belt/water pump plus the suspension install and an alignment sheet would move documentation and price_value up materially.
A clean independent PPI in San Diego — dry underbody, healthy transmission and transfer case fluid, no stored SAI or AVS codes, sound frame — would make this a credible capability buy.
Evidence of a permanent check-engine/AVS light, incomplete smog readiness, coolant in the transmission, or meaningful frame corrosion would end it.
Negotiating toward the $12,000–14,000 band that 200k-plus GX470s actually trade in, given the absent records, would substantially improve the risk-adjusted value.
Discovery that the photographed silver car with stock wheels and ride height is this VIN — i.e. the build described is not on this truck — would be disqualifying until resolved.
evidence.mission_note: As a capability buy this is the correct shape — body-on-frame V8, low range, roof rack and a flat cargo bay the RX 350 cannot match — but it also overlaps the RX as the family hauler, so it only earns its place if the off-pavement/camping capability is genuinely wanted rather than nice to have. evidence.rationale: This is a plausible, well-shaped GX470 whose entire case rests on unverified seller prose. The ad lists exactly the right work for a 221,000-mile 2UZ truck — timing belt, water pump, serpentine belt, CV axles, brakes front and rear, and elimination of the failure-prone rear air suspension in favour of an Old Man Emu 2-inch setup on Method wheels and BFG KO2s — but supplies no invoice, no date and no mileage for any of it, so the model-critical timing belt and suspension items sit at claimed_only and rust, warning lights and cooling/leak history are simply missing. The identity side of documentation is fine: VIN, stock number, equipment list, a single $16,995 price with dealer fees included, and a named San Diego dealer with published hours; the maintenance side is empty. Pricing is the other pressure point: recent comps put 200k-plus GX470s at $8,400–$11,600 while $16,000–$17,000 has been buying 90k–160k-mile cars, and the profile's own market note says modified builds trade at a discount to documented stock examples. The photo of the silver car shows an even, sensible lift, four matching all-terrains and no visible damage, which is reassuring as far as it goes; the attached set also contains several other GX470s, so confirm which images are this VIN. Logistics are genuinely easy — 372 miles, a physical lot, a straightforward PPI and drive home — and Toyota/Lexus mechanicals plus Jason's mechanic's preferences make the mileage a yellow flag rather than a stop. Nothing here is disqualifying, but nothing is proven either, and unknown is not a positive. The path forward is receipts and an independent inspection before any money moves, with the price renegotiated if the records do not materialise.

For a 126k-mile 1UR-FE truck whose two big-ticket risks (secondary air injection, KDSS) are both diagnostic questions, this is thin.

The dealer's own board shows a 124k-mile 2014 at $29,995 and a 147k-mile 2015 at $27,995, so this unit is priced at the top of its own lot. The premium is entirely the ICON/GOBI/ARB build, which is dealer-installed cost that does not return at resale, and the asking price alone exceeds Jason's $27,000 max before tax, registration, or any catch-up work — all-in lands near the $33,000 defeats-purpose line.

Paying a modified-truck premium to add that character, while the BMW replacement budget is what is actually under pressure, weakens the fit rather than the concept.

logistics.rationale: San Diego is roughly 455 miles from Carmel — a comfortable fly-or-drive day, and a good car drives itself home on new tires. KDSS confirmation with a measured lean of under ~1 inch and no hydraulic weeping, plus a KDSS-correct ICON install invoice and alignment sheet, would validate the build.

evidence.mission_note: As pure capability this is exactly the utility_capability brief — a lifted, rack-and-awning GX460 does dogs, gear and light off-road duty the RX 350 cannot — but it is a second large Lexus SUV bought at a builder's retail premium, and at $31,995 it consumes the budget that is actually needed to retire the 335i. In accelerated_bridge mode it only makes sense at a materially lower out-the-door number with the air-injection and KDSS questions answered on paper.
evidence.rationale: The blocking issue is price, not the car: $31,995 for a base-trim 2014 with 126,000 miles sits above every relevant comp — a 63.5k-mile 2013 Convenience at $25,040, a 128.5k-mile 2017 Premium at $23,900, and the dealer's own 124k-mile 2014 at $29,995 — and it exceeds Jason's $27,000 max before tax and registration. The premium is a dealer-installed ICON Stage 2 / GOBI / ARB / Method build; the parts are quality and the photos corroborate the lift, matched bronze wheels and fresh KO3s, but that money does not come back at resale. Documentation is the other weakness: 'FULLY SERVICED', 'REAR BRAKE JOB', '1 ORIGINAL OWNER' and 'AMAZING SHAPE' are all seller prose with no receipts, no attached history report, no odometer photo and no scan data. Both model-critical mechanical questions are entirely unaddressed — secondary air injection (P2440/P2442, expensive and a California smog-fail item) and KDSS lean/leak status, which matters doubly because a Stage 2 lift on a KDSS chassis requires the KDSS-specific kit. Rust is likely a non-issue given San Diego provenance, but that is inference from location, not an underbody inspection, and no frame photos were captured. Logistics are the strong point: 455 in-state miles, a storefront dealer who must supply smog, and a straightforward PPI at a San Diego specialist. Mission-wise it delivers real capability the RX 350 lacks, but it is a second big Lexus SUV purchased at the top of its market while the 335i replacement budget is the actual constraint. Worth a scan-and-receipts conversation; not worth $31,995.
evidence.next_action: Email Miramar Motorsports asking for a cold full-system OBD scan photo with readiness monitors, the ICON install and service invoices, the full Carfax PDF, and written confirmation that an off-site independent PPI is allowed — and open at an out-the-door number in the $25,000–$26,000 range consistent with the comps.

evidence.rationale: This is an attractive, correctly specified S52 M Roadster priced as though it were a documented one. The bad news is that the profile's two decisive items for this model are entirely absent. There is no cooling-system documentation on a 25-year-old car whose plastics fail on age rather than mileage, and there is nothing at all — no underbody photo, no trunk-floor image, no lift inspection — covering the rear subframe and differential-mount ears, the failure that separates a $28,000 M Roadster from a project. Documentation, not the odometer, is what earns a premium on these cars, and this listing has the odometer only. Everything hinges on a specialist lift inspection and on the price coming down toward what documented cars actually trade for.
evidence.next_action: Call South Pointe Honda and ask two questions before anything else: will they release the car to a named Tulsa BMW independent for a lift PPI focused on the rear subframe and cooling system, and what reconditioning work order and prior-owner records exist for stock YLC91663 — then book the inspection only if both answers are yes.

The seller is a Chrysler franchise store, not a Lexus specialist, and a $499 recon line implies a safety pass rather than a service, so nothing in the file substitutes for a lift. What is entirely absent is the second half — maintenance and condition evidence. Zero receipts, no cooling-system history, no undercarriage or trunk-floor photographs, no scan data, no statement that records accompany the car. On a Z3 M the market pays for documentation more than for mileage, and there is none here.

condition.rationale: The visible cosmetics are genuinely good: Imola Red paint with clean, undistorted reflections across the hood and doors, straight panel gaps at the front, unmarked M double-spoke wheels, no curb rash on the front wheel close-up, clean black interior with the top stowed. But everything that actually determines whether this is a good Z3 M is unexamined here — rear subframe/trunk-floor welds, differential mount, cooling plastics, soft-top mechanism, trailing-arm bushings, rear shock mounts, tire dates. 30,959 miles across 28 years and five owners means the car has sat far more than it has driven, which is hard on seals, hoses, tires and the top, and there is no service evidence to offset that. price_value.rationale: At $21,353 with fees included, this sits mid-pack against the comps: a 29,120-mile 1999 sold on BaT at $23,500, a 34,400-mile 2000 sold at $27,000 on Cars & Bids, a 14,600-mile 1999 sold at $27,995 in Mission Viejo, while a 33,000-mile 2000 went reserve-not-met at $14,600 and mid-mileage roadsters trade $17,900-$24,000. The offset is that with no records, cooling refresh and a rear-structure inspection have to be priced in as near-certain spend, and undocumented Z3 Ms resell to enthusiasts at a discount.

mission_fit.rationale: As a future_keeper this is squarely on the profile list — a factory-manual S52 M Roadster, the more robust of the two Z3 M engines, no rod-bearing exposure, in a desirable colour. Attractive as a keeper, in tension with the accelerated_bridge cash-preservation logic, and it would leave Jason still shopping for the actual bridge.

logistics.rationale: Joliet, IL is a fly-out-and-drive-home proposition, which the buyer accepts, and a fixed dealer address makes a specialist PPI arrangeable in principle — Chicago has good BMW independents who know the Z3 M rear structure. Against that: PPI access is not offered or confirmed, the dealer is a high-volume exotic house with a 3.3/5 rating over 124 reviews and no evident interest in this car's history, and a 1998 gasoline car imported into California needs a passing smog certificate with no readiness or test data provided. emotional_spec_fit.rationale: Imola Red over black, factory five-speed, S52 M Roadster with the fender gills, roadster hood and the chrome-ringed M kidney — this is exactly the character the buyer likes, and it is one of the cars named in his own shortlist family.
